recipes.name: Ful medames (stewed fava beans)
recipes.description: Cairo's everyday breakfast: slow-cooked fava beans warmed and roughly mashed with garlic, cumin, lemon and plenty of olive oil, topped with tomato and parsley and scooped up with warm flatbread.

ingredients.name: Bean liquid from the can, or water
Garlic
ingredients.prep: crushed to a paste with a pinch of salt

ingredients.name: Tahini
ingredients.prep: loosened with lemon juice and water

steps.t: Tip the beans and about 100 ml of their liquid (or water) into the saucepan. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the beans are hot right through and soft enough to crush easily against the side of the pan.

While the beans heat, crush the garlic with a pinch of salt to a smooth paste using the flat of a knife or a mortar. Dice the tomatoes, chop the parsley and warm the bread in a dry frying pan or a low oven.

Take the pan off the heat and mash the beans roughly with the masher or a fork. Cairenes like a mixture of creamy purée and half-broken beans rather than a smooth paste. If it looks stiff, loosen it with a splash of hot water: it should slump softly off a spoon.
Stir in the garlic paste, cumin, chilli, lemon juice and half the olive oil. Taste and season with salt. Good ful is bright with lemon and garlic, so add more of either if it tastes flat.

Spread the ful into a shallow bowl or onto plates and make a well in the centre with the back of a spoon. Pour the remaining olive oil into the well and over the top, then scatter over the diced tomato, parsley and a final pinch of cumin.
Serve warm with the bread for scooping, with sliced raw onion, pickles, a drizzle of tahini or halved boiled eggs if you like. In Cairo it is eaten alongside ta'ameya for a full breakfast.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated without the toppings.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of hot water, stirring, until steaming hot.
notes: To cook dried beans: soak 220 g small dried fava beans overnight, then simmer in plenty of unsalted water, partly covered, for 2–3 hours (or about 40 minutes in a pressure cooker) until completely soft. Add salt only at the end, or the skins stay tough.

recipes.name: Ta'ameya (Egyptian falafel)
recipes.description: Egypt's green falafel, made from soaked split fava beans instead of chickpeas and blended with a big bunch of herbs, so the fritters are bright green and fluffy inside. Rolled in sesame and fried until crisp.

ingredients.name: Dried split (skinned) fava beans
ingredients.prep: soaked in cold water for 12–24 hours, drained

steps.t: At least 12 hours ahead, cover the split fava beans with plenty of cold water (they will roughly double in size) and leave to soak, changing the water once if your kitchen is warm. Drain them very well in a colander and pat dry with a tea towel: wet beans make fritters that fall apart in the oil.

Put the drained beans, onion, spring onions, garlic, chilli, coriander, parsley and dill into the food processor. Pulse in short bursts, scraping down the sides every few pulses, until finely ground, bright green and holding together when squeezed, like damp sand. Stop before it turns into a smooth paste.
Tip into a bowl and mix in the cumin, ground coriander, salt and pepper. Cover and chill for 30 minutes so the mixture firms up; it is much easier to shape cold.

Pour the oil into the deep pan to a depth of about 5 cm, no more than one-third full, and heat it to 175 °C, or until a pinch of the mixture sizzles at once and floats up. Just before frying, stir the bicarbonate of soda into the mixture: it starts working straight away and makes the ta'ameya light inside.

With wet hands, shape walnut-sized pieces into flat discs about 5 cm wide and 1.5 cm thick and press one side into the sesame seeds. Lower 6–8 at a time into the oil, sesame side up, without crowding the pan.

Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown and crisp. Break the first one open: the inside should be fluffy and green, not raw and pasty. Lift out with the slotted spoon onto kitchen paper and let the oil come back to 175 °C before the next batch.
Serve hot, tucked into baladi bread or pita with tahini sauce, sliced tomato, cucumber and pickles, or alongside a bowl of ful medames for a Cairo breakfast.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh. The raw mixture (before the bicarbonate of soda goes in) keeps 2 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp fried ta'ameya in a 200 °C oven for 6–8 minutes.
notes: Use split, skinned fava beans (sold as peeled or split broad beans); whole brown fava beans must be skinned by hand after soaking.
Never use cooked or canned beans: the raw soaked beans are what hold the fritters together.

recipes.name: Hawawshi (spiced beef baked in bread)
recipes.description: Egyptian street food: round flatbreads split open and filled with a thin layer of minced beef spiced with onion, green pepper, chilli and allspice, brushed with oil and baked until the bread crackles and soaks up the juices.

ingredients.name: Baladi bread or thick pita, about 18 cm

steps.t: Heat the oven to 220 °C with the baking tray inside. Grate the onion on the coarse side of the box grater, then squeeze it hard in your hands over the sink to remove most of its juice; wet onion makes the filling and the bread soggy.

In the bowl, combine the beef, squeezed onion, green pepper, chilli, garlic, parsley, tomato paste, all the spices and the salt. Knead with your hand for 1–2 minutes until the mixture turns sticky and evenly speckled. Fry a teaspoonful in a small pan and taste it if you want to check the seasoning.

Cut each bread around about three-quarters of its edge to open it like a book, leaving a hinge. Spread a quarter of the meat inside in an even layer about 1 cm thick, right to the edges, then press the bread closed firmly so the meat sticks to both sides.
Brush both sides of each filled bread generously with the oil or melted samna; this is what makes the crust crackle as it bakes.

Lay the breads on the hot tray and bake for 10 minutes, then turn them over and bake for another 10–12 minutes, until the bread is deep golden, dark in places and crisp, and the meat is sizzling at the edges. A thermometer pushed into the filling should read at least 71 °C.
Rest for 2 minutes, then cut each hawawshi into quarters with a serrated knife. Serve hot with tahini sauce, pickled vegetables (torshi) and a chopped tomato and cucumber salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot oven or a dry frying pan so the bread crisps again, until the filling is steaming hot.
notes: In Alexandria hawawshi is often made by wrapping the meat in a thin homemade dough instead of bread.

recipes.name: Om Ali (Egyptian bread pudding)
recipes.description: Egypt's favourite warm pudding: crisp baked puff pastry broken into a dish with nuts, raisins and coconut, soaked in sweet hot milk, topped with cream and baked until bubbling and golden.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Unroll the puff pastry onto the tray lined with baking paper and prick it all over with a fork. Bake for 15–18 minutes until well puffed, deep golden and crisp right through; pale, underbaked pastry turns soggy in the milk.

Let the pastry cool for 5 minutes, then break it into rough 3–4 cm pieces with your hands. Scatter half over the base of the baking dish, then half the almonds, pistachios, raisins and coconut. Repeat with the rest of the pastry and the fruit and nuts, keeping back a small handful of nuts for the top.

Meanwhile, warm the milk and sugar in the saucepan over medium heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves and the milk is steaming with small bubbles around the edge, 5–6 minutes; don't let it boil over. Stir in the vanilla.
Pour the hot milk evenly over the pastry and press down gently with a spoon so every piece is moistened. Leave to soak for 5 minutes: the pastry should soften but still keep some texture.

Turn the oven up to 220 °C. Pour the cream over the top in a thin layer and scatter with the reserved nuts. Bake on the top shelf for 10–12 minutes, until the surface is bubbling and patched with golden-brown spots.
Rest for 5 minutes, dust with cinnamon if you like and serve warm in bowls, scooping down to the soft, milky layers underneath.

recipes.storage: Best on the day; leftovers keep 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a low oven or the microwave with a splash of milk.
notes: Some families use torn croissants or baked roqaq bread instead of puff pastry.

recipes.name: Chicken tagine with preserved lemon and olives (djaj mqualli)
recipes.description: Fez-style djaj mqualli: chicken braised with grated onion, ginger, saffron and turmeric until it falls from the bone, then finished with salty preserved lemon and green olives in a thick golden sauce.
equipment: Tagine or wide heavy lidded casserole

ingredients.name: Chicken legs and thighs on the bone, skinned
Salt
ingredients.prep: more to taste at the end

ingredients.name: Preserved lemon
ingredients.prep: pulp discarded, rind cut into strips

steps.t: In the tagine or casserole, mix the chicken with the grated onion, garlic, ginger, turmeric, pepper, the saffron and its water, the oil, the butter and the ½ teaspoon of salt; the preserved lemon and olives add more salt later. Rub the spices well into the meat and leave for 15–30 minutes if you have time.

Set the pot over medium heat (use a diffuser under a clay tagine and keep the heat low to medium). Cook for 10 minutes, turning the chicken, until the onion softens and the spices smell warm and toasty. The meat colours only lightly, which is right for this pale golden dish.

Tie the coriander and parsley sprigs into a small bundle with kitchen string and tuck it in among the chicken. Pour in the water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook gently for 45 minutes, turning the pieces halfway, until the chicken is very tender and pulls easily from the bone.

Meanwhile, rinse the preserved lemon, scoop out and discard the pulp, and cut the rind into thin strips. Rinse the olives; if they taste very salty, simmer them in fresh water for 2 minutes and drain.

Lift the chicken onto a plate and remove the herb bundle. Boil the sauce uncovered over medium-high heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring and mashing the soft onion into it, until it reduces to a thick, glossy, golden sauce that coats a spoon.

Return the chicken to the pot, add the preserved lemon and olives and spoon the sauce over. Simmer for 5 minutes so the flavours mingle. The thickest piece should reach 74 °C with clear juices. Taste, and only then add lemon juice or salt if it needs it.
Serve straight from the tagine with khobz (Moroccan round bread) for scooping up the sauce.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Preserved lemons are whole lemons cured in salt and sold in jars. If you can't find them, use the grated zest of 1 lemon and an extra tablespoon of juice, though the flavour is less deep.

recipes.name: Kefta mkaouara (meatball and egg tagine)
recipes.description: Small cumin-and-herb meatballs simmered in a spiced fresh tomato sauce, with eggs cracked into the pan at the end and cooked until just set. A Moroccan weeknight favourite eaten straight from the pot with bread.
equipment: Tagine or wide lidded frying pan, 26–28 cm

ingredients.name: Minced beef or lamb (or half and half)

steps.t: Make the kefta: put the beef, grated onion, parsley, coriander, cumin, paprika, salt and pepper in the bowl and knead with your hand for 2 minutes, until the mixture turns sticky and holds together. With wet hands, roll it into balls the size of a large cherry, about 2.5 cm; you should get 25–30.

Heat the oil in the tagine or frying pan over medium heat. Add the chopped onion and cook, stirring often, for 5 minutes until soft and translucent, then add the garlic and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.

Add the grated tomatoes, tomato paste, cumin, paprika, cayenne, salt and water. Bring to a simmer and cook uncovered for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce has thickened slightly and no longer tastes raw.
Lay the meatballs in the sauce in a single layer. Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes, turning them once halfway, until cooked through: cut one open to check there is no pink left in the centre.

If the sauce is still thin, simmer uncovered for 3–5 minutes more; it should be thick enough to hold a well. Make four gaps between the meatballs and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook over low heat for 5–7 minutes, until the whites are set and opaque and the yolks are still soft, or longer if you like them firm.
Scatter with the chopped coriander and a pinch of cumin and bring the pan to the table. Serve with plenty of khobz or crusty bread to tear and scoop up the meatballs, egg and sauce.

recipes.storage: Best fresh; the meatballs in sauce (without eggs) keep 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Harira (lamb, lentil and chickpea soup)
recipes.description: The soup that breaks the fast across Morocco during Ramadan: lamb, lentils and chickpeas simmered in a tomato and herb broth spiced with ginger, cinnamon and pepper, then thickened to a velvety finish with a flour slurry.
equipment: Large heavy soup pot (at least 5 litres)

steps.t: Put the lamb, onion, celery, half the chopped coriander and parsley, the oil, butter, ginger, turmeric, cinnamon, pepper and 1 teaspoon of the salt into the large pot. Cook over medium heat, stirring, for 8–10 minutes until the meat has lost its raw colour and the onions are soft and fragrant.

Add the drained chickpeas, the blended tomatoes and the tomato paste and cook, stirring, for 5 minutes until the tomatoes darken slightly. Pour in the 2.5 litres of water, bring to the boil, then cover and simmer gently for 45 minutes, until the chickpeas are nearly tender.

Add the rinsed lentils and the remaining salt and simmer, partly covered, for 25–30 minutes more, until the lentils and chickpeas are completely soft and the lamb is tender. Top up with hot water if the soup has reduced to much less than about 2.5 litres.
Make the tadouira: whisk the flour into the 250 ml of cold water until completely smooth, like thin cream. Leave it to rest for a few minutes, then whisk again just before using.

Add the vermicelli to the simmering soup and cook for 3 minutes. Then, stirring the soup constantly, pour in the flour mixture in a slow, thin stream. Keep stirring and simmering for 8–10 minutes, until the soup turns silky, coats the back of a spoon and no longer tastes of raw flour. Stir often from now on, as thickened soup catches on the bottom easily.
Stir in the rest of the chopped herbs and taste for salt and pepper. If using the eggs, drizzle them in slowly while stirring so they set in fine ribbons, then take the pot off the heat.
Ladle into bowls and serve with lemon wedges to squeeze over. At iftar, harira is eaten with dates, hard-boiled eggs and honeyed chebakia pastries.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen. It thickens as it stands.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat, stirring, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Soak the chickpeas in plenty of cold water for 8–12 hours. For a quicker harira, use a 400 g can of chickpeas, drained, and add them with the lentils.

recipes.name: Zaalouk (smoky aubergine and tomato salad)
recipes.description: A soft, smoky cooked salad of charred aubergine and fresh tomato, simmered with garlic, cumin and paprika until jammy, finished with herbs and lemon. Served warm or at room temperature with bread.

steps.t: Prick the aubergines a few times with a knife and set them directly over a medium gas flame. Turn them with tongs every couple of minutes for 12–15 minutes, until the skin is blackened all over and the flesh has completely collapsed. Without a gas hob, halve them and roast cut side down on an oiled tray at 220 °C for 30–35 minutes.

Put the charred aubergines in a bowl, cover and leave for 5 minutes to steam, which loosens the skin. Peel off and discard the skin (a few black flecks add flavour), pull out any long seed strands and chop the flesh roughly.

Warm the olive oil in the frying pan over medium heat, add the garlic and stir for 1 minute until fragrant but not coloured. Add the grated tomatoes, paprika, cumin, cayenne and salt and simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the tomato has thickened and darkened.

Add the aubergine and half the herbs and mash everything together with a fork or potato masher. Cook over medium-low heat for 10–12 minutes, stirring and mashing often, until thick and jammy, with the oil separating at the edges.

Stir in the lemon juice and the rest of the herbs, taste for salt and leave to cool a little. Serve warm or at room temperature with bread, as part of a spread of Moroccan salads, or alongside grilled meat or fish.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated; the flavour improves overnight. Serve at room temperature.

recipes.name: Msemen (square laminated flatbread)
recipes.description: Morocco's flaky griddle bread: a soft dough stretched paper-thin, sprinkled with semolina and butter, folded into a square and cooked until crisp and golden in layers. Eaten warm with honey and mint tea.

steps.t: Mix the flour, 100 g semolina, salt, sugar and yeast in the bowl. Add the warm water a little at a time, mixing with your hand, until a soft dough forms. Knead on the work surface for 8–10 minutes until very smooth, elastic and soft, as soft as an earlobe; add a few drops more water if it feels firm.

Oil your hands and divide the dough into 8 equal balls, smoothing each one. Set them on an oiled tray, brush with oil, cover with a cloth and rest for 15 minutes so the gluten relaxes and the dough stretches without tearing.

Mix the oil and soft butter. Generously oil the work surface and your hands. Flatten one ball, then push and stretch it outwards with your fingertips into a very thin, almost translucent sheet about 25 cm across. A few small holes are fine.

Dot the sheet with a little butter mixture and sprinkle with semolina. Fold the top third down and the bottom third up, like a letter, to make a long strip. Dot and sprinkle again, then fold the two ends into the middle to make a square of about 8 cm. Repeat with the remaining balls and rest the squares for 10 minutes.

Heat the frying pan over medium heat. With oiled fingers, pat a square out to about 15 cm, keeping it even. Cook for 2–3 minutes per side, turning two or three times and pressing gently, until both sides are golden and crisp and the layers have puffed slightly. Too high a heat burns the outside before the layers inside cook.
Stack the cooked msemen under a cloth to keep them soft while you cook the rest. Serve warm with honey melted with a little butter, with amlou or soft cheese, and a glass of mint tea.

recipes.storage: Best fresh. Cool completely, then keep wrapped for 1 day or freeze between sheets of baking paper for up to 2 months.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a dry frying pan over medium heat for about 1 minute per side.
notes: For msemen m'amar, spread a little cooked filling of onion, parsley, cumin and paprika over the sheet before the final fold.

recipes.name: Atay (Moroccan mint tea)
recipes.description: Gunpowder green tea brewed strong with a big handful of fresh spearmint and sugar, poured from a height to raise a foam. Served all day in small glasses as the gesture of welcome in every Moroccan home.
equipment: Metal teapot that can go on the hob

ingredients.name: Fresh spearmint
ingredients.prep: a large handful of sprigs, rinsed

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil. Put the tea into the teapot, pour in about 100 ml of the boiling water, swirl for 20 seconds and pour this first glass into a cup. Keep it: Moroccans call it the spirit of the tea.
Pour another 100 ml of boiling water over the leaves, swirl and pour it away this time. This quick rinse washes away dust and some of the bitterness.

Return the reserved first glass to the pot and add the sugar and the remaining boiling water. Set the pot over low heat for 3–4 minutes, until it just begins to murmur; don't let it boil hard or the tea turns bitter.
Take the pot off the heat, push the mint sprigs down into it and leave to steep for 3–4 minutes.

Pour a glass and tip it back into the pot two or three times to mix the sugar through, then taste one and adjust the sugar. Serve by pouring from as high above the glasses as you dare, so each one gets a crown of foam.

recipes.storage: Drink fresh; tea left sitting on the leaves turns bitter.
notes: Sugar is traditionally generous; halve it if you prefer, or serve it without and pass sugar separately.

recipes.name: Tunisian chakchouka (peppers, tomato and eggs with harissa)
recipes.description: Tunisia's own shakshuka: plenty of sweet and hot peppers slowly softened with onion, tomato, garlic and harissa, seasoned with caraway and coriander (tabil), then finished with eggs set gently in the sauce.
equipment: Wide lidded frying pan or sauté pan, 28 cm

ingredients.name: Green and red peppers (or long Tunisian peppers)

steps.t: Heat the olive oil in the wide pan over medium heat. Add the onion and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent.

Add the pepper strips and chilli with a pinch of the salt. Cook for 12–15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the peppers are soft, sweet and collapsing, with a few browned edges. Take your time here: the slowly cooked peppers are the heart of chakchouka.

Push the vegetables aside, add the garlic, harissa and tomato paste to the cleared space and fry for 1 minute, stirring, until the paste darkens and smells toasty. This frying of the paste in oil takes away its raw edge.

Stir in the tomatoes, coriander, caraway, paprika, the rest of the salt and the water. Simmer uncovered for 8–10 minutes, until the tomatoes have broken down into a thick sauce that coats the peppers and a spoon drawn across the pan leaves a trail. Taste and add more harissa if you like it hotter.

Reduce the heat to low. Make six wells in the sauce and crack an egg into each. Cover and cook for 5–7 minutes, until the whites are set and opaque and the yolks are still soft; for firm yolks, cook a few minutes longer. Some Tunisian cooks prefer to stir the eggs through the sauce to scramble them softly, which is just as traditional.
Scatter with parsley and serve straight from the pan with crusty bread, black olives and a small dish of extra harissa.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; the pepper sauce alone keeps 3 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the sauce until bubbling before adding fresh eggs.
notes: Tunisian cooks often add diced potato, courgette or a little merguez with the peppers; for merguez, use halal beef or lamb sausage and cook it through before adding the eggs.

recipes.name: Lablabi (Tunisian chickpea and garlic soup)
recipes.description: Tunis's favourite winter breakfast and street soup: chickpeas in a garlicky cumin broth ladled over torn stale bread, then topped at the table with harissa, olive oil, lemon, capers and a soft egg.

steps.t: Put the chickpeas, water, the 4 crushed garlic cloves, 1 teaspoon of the cumin and the salt in the saucepan. Bring to the boil, then simmer gently for 15 minutes, until the broth tastes of garlic and the chickpeas are very soft. Crush a handful of chickpeas against the side of the pan to give the broth a little body.

Meanwhile, soft-boil the eggs: lower them into a small pan of simmering water and cook for 6 minutes, then cool under cold running water and peel. In Tunis the egg is often cracked raw into the bowl and cooked by the hot broth; soft-boiling is safer and gives the same creamy yolk.
Stir the pounded garlic paste and the remaining cumin into the soup and taste for salt; the broth should be well seasoned and fragrant. Keep it at a bare simmer.
Divide the torn bread between the bowls. Ladle the chickpeas and plenty of boiling broth over the bread so it softens and soaks it up.
Top each bowl with a halved soft egg, a spoonful of harissa, capers and the tuna if using, then pour a generous tablespoon of olive oil over and add a pinch of cumin.
Serve at once with lemon wedges. Everyone stirs their own bowl, breaking the yolk and mixing in the harissa and lemon, so the bread turns into a thick, spicy porridge.

recipes.storage: Keep the broth and chickpeas separately from the bread and toppings; refrigerate for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: With dried chickpeas, soak 300 g overnight and simmer them in the water with the garlic for 1–1½ hours until very soft before continuing.

recipes.name: Brik à l'œuf (crisp egg-filled pastry)
recipes.description: Tunisia's iconic starter: a whole egg cracked onto a little potato, parsley, onion and capers in paper-thin pastry, folded and fried until shatteringly crisp while the yolk stays soft. Eaten by hand with a squeeze of lemon.

steps.t: Mix the mashed potato with the onion, parsley, capers, pepper and salt (and the tuna and cheese, if using). Divide into four portions. Have everything, including the eggs and a plate lined with kitchen paper, ready by the stove: brik is assembled and fried in under a minute.
Pour the oil into the frying pan to a depth of about 1.5 cm and heat over medium-high heat to 180 °C, when a scrap of pastry sizzles and turns golden in 30 seconds.

If using filo, lay one sheet on a plate and another on top. Spread a portion of filling on one half in a ring, leaving a well in the centre about 5 cm from the edge. Crack an egg into the well, then fold the empty half of the pastry over to make a half-moon (or fold the corners in to make a triangle) and press the edges lightly.

Slide the brik straight into the hot oil, using the plate to help. Fry for 45–60 seconds, spooning hot oil over the top, then turn carefully with the fish slice and fry for another 30–45 seconds, until both sides are deep golden and blistered. The white will be set and the yolk still runny; fry a minute longer on a lower heat for a firm yolk.
Lift onto the kitchen paper to drain for a few seconds and repeat with the remaining briks, letting the oil come back to temperature in between.
Serve immediately with lemon wedges to squeeze over. Hold the brik by its corners and bite carefully into the yolk.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within minutes of frying; brik does not keep.
notes: Filo is drier and thinner than Tunisian malsouka, so use two sheets together and work quickly before it dries.

recipes.name: Chorba frik (lamb and cracked green wheat soup)
recipes.description: The Ramadan soup of Algeria and eastern Tunisia: lamb, chickpeas and frik (smoky cracked green wheat) simmered in a tomato broth with coriander, mint and cinnamon until thick and comforting.

ingredients.name: Frik (cracked green wheat), or coarse bulgur

steps.t: Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat and add the lamb, onion, half the coriander, the cinnamon stick, paprika, pepper, ras el hanout and 1 teaspoon of the salt. Cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until the meat has lost its pink colour and the onion is soft and smells sweet.
Add the grated tomatoes and tomato paste and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until the mixture darkens to a deep red and the oil starts to separate around the edges.

Add the drained chickpeas and the hot water and bring to the boil, skimming off any grey foam. Cover and simmer over low heat for 40 minutes, until the lamb is tender and the chickpeas are nearly soft.

Rinse the frik in a sieve and add it to the pot with the remaining salt, stirring well so it doesn't clump. Simmer, partly covered, for 20–25 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes as it thickens, until the grains are swollen and tender and the soup has a thick, creamy body. Add a splash of hot water if it becomes too thick to pour from a ladle.
Stir in the dried mint, rubbing it between your palms to release its scent, and most of the remaining coriander. Simmer for 2 minutes, then remove the cinnamon stick and taste for salt and pepper.
Ladle into bowls, scatter with the last of the coriander and serve with lemon wedges. At iftar it is eaten with bourek pastries and bread.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen; it thickens as it stands.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat, stirring, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Frik is young durum wheat that is roasted and cracked, giving a smoky flavour; it is sold in North African shops. Coarse bulgur is the closest substitute.

recipes.name: Rechta (steamed noodles with chicken in white sauce)
recipes.description: The festive dish of Algiers: thin flat noodles steamed until silky, served under a pale cinnamon-scented broth of chicken, chickpeas and turnips. Cooked for Mawlid, Ashura and family celebrations.
equipment: Couscoussier (or a large pot with a snug steamer basket)

steps.t: Put the chicken, oil, butter, grated onion, cinnamon stick, pepper and 1 teaspoon of the salt in the base of the couscoussier. Cook over medium heat, turning the pieces, for 10 minutes until the onion has softened and the chicken looks opaque all over; it should stay pale, not brown, for a white sauce.
Add the drained chickpeas and the water and bring to the boil, skimming off any foam. Lower the heat, cover and simmer for 45 minutes, until the chickpeas are nearly tender.

Meanwhile, tip the dried noodles into a large bowl, drizzle with 1 tablespoon of the oil and rub them gently between your hands so every strand is coated; this stops them sticking in the steamer. Line the steamer basket with a damp tea towel if its holes are large.

Add the turnips and the remaining salt to the sauce. Set the steamer basket of noodles on top of the pot, sealing the join with a twisted strip of damp cloth if steam escapes. Steam for 15 minutes from the moment steam rises through the noodles.

Tip the noodles back into the bowl, sprinkle with about 150 ml of the hot broth and the remaining oil and gently separate the strands with a fork. Return to the steamer for a second 15 minutes, until tender and silky, with no hard core when you bite one. Check the turnips: they should be soft and the chicken should reach 74 °C.

Toss the steamed noodles with the butter and spread them in the serving dish. Arrange the chicken, turnips and chickpeas on top and ladle over plenty of the hot broth, so the noodles drink it up. Dust with ground cinnamon.
Serve hot, with a jug of extra broth on the side for pouring over at the table.

recipes.storage: Keep the sauce and the noodles separately; refrigerate for up to 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the sauce until steaming hot; re-steam or microwave the noodles with a splash of broth.
notes: If your rechta packet suggests boiling, cook the noodles in salted water for the time on the pack, drain and toss with butter instead of steaming.
Some families add a few courgette pieces to the sauce in the last 15 minutes.

recipes.name: Shorba libiya (Libyan lamb and orzo soup)
recipes.description: Libya's everyday and Ramadan soup: lamb and chickpeas in a deep red tomato broth spiced with turmeric and hararat, thickened with orzo and finished with dried mint and lemon.

ingredients.name: Hararat or bzaar (Libyan spice mix)
ingredients.prep: or a mix of cumin, cinnamon and coriander

steps.t: Heat the oil in the pot over medium-high heat. Add the lamb and onion and cook for 8 minutes, stirring often, until the meat is browned in patches and the onion is soft and golden.

Lower the heat to medium, add the tomato paste, turmeric, hararat, chilli, pepper and 1 teaspoon of the salt and fry, stirring constantly, for 2–3 minutes, until the paste turns from bright to a deep brick red and the spices smell toasty. Frying the paste well is what gives shorba its rich colour and taste.
Pour in the hot water, scraping up anything stuck to the bottom, and bring to the boil. Cover and simmer gently for 40 minutes, until the lamb is tender.

Add the drained chickpeas and the remaining salt and simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in the orzo and simmer for 10–12 minutes, stirring often so it doesn't settle and stick, until the pasta is soft and has thickened the soup slightly.

Stir in the parsley and the dried mint, rubbing the mint between your palms over the pot to release its aroma. Simmer for 1 minute, then taste: the soup should be peppery, a little spicy and well salted. Thin with a splash of hot water if it is too thick.
Serve hot in bowls with lemon wedges for squeezing over; the lemon is essential. During Ramadan it is the first dish after dates and milk, followed by bourek pastries.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; the orzo keeps absorbing broth.
recipes.reheating: Loosen with water and reheat, stirring, until steaming hot throughout.

recipes.name: Bazeen (barley dough with lamb and tomato stew)
recipes.description: Libya's national dish: a smooth dome of stiff barley dough set in the middle of a wide dish and surrounded by a spicy tomato stew of lamb, potatoes and hard-boiled eggs. Shared from one plate and eaten with the right hand.
equipment: Large heavy pot for the stew

steps.t: Make the stew: heat the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat, add the lamb and onion and cook, turning, for 8–10 minutes until the meat is browned on several sides and the onion is golden.

Lower the heat, add the tomato paste, turmeric, hararat, chilli, pepper and salt and fry for 3 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste turns deep red and the oil comes through. Pour in the hot water, bring to the boil, cover and simmer gently for 60 minutes. Add the potatoes and simmer for 25–30 minutes more, until the lamb is very tender and a knife slides easily into the potatoes. The sauce should be thick but still pourable.

While the stew simmers, make the dough: bring the 1 litre of water and the salt to the boil in the heavy saucepan. Tip in the barley flour all at once in a mound, without stirring. Cover, lower the heat and let it steam for 15 minutes so the flour cooks from below.

Uncover and beat the mixture hard with the wooden spoon or stick, pressing and folding it against the side of the pan, for 5–10 minutes, until it forms one stiff, smooth, elastic mass with no dry flour. It is hard work; brace the pan with a cloth. If it is too stiff to work, add a few tablespoons of the hot stew liquid.

Cover and cook the dough over the lowest heat for 10 minutes more, then turn it onto a wet board. With wet hands, knead it briefly and shape it into a smooth, high dome. Add the hard-boiled eggs to the stew to warm through for 5 minutes.
Set the dome in the centre of the serving platter. Ladle the sauce all around it, arrange the lamb, potatoes and halved eggs in the sauce, and place lemon halves and green chillies around the edge.

To eat, everyone squeezes lemon over the sauce, pinches off pieces of dough from the dome with their right hand, dips them in the stew and eats them with the meat and potatoes. Serve at once while the dough is hot and soft.

recipes.storage: The stew keeps 3 days refrigerated; the dough is best made fresh, as it hardens on cooling.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Barley flour gives bazeen its nutty taste and slightly grainy texture; some families mix in a quarter of plain wheat flour to make the dough smoother and easier to shape.

recipes.name: Sudanese ful (fava beans with sesame oil and white cheese)
recipes.description: Khartoum's breakfast staple: hot fava beans mashed with mild sesame oil, cumin and salt, then piled with crumbled white cheese, tomato, onion, green chilli and rocket, and eaten with fresh bread.

ingredients.name: Sudanese white cheese (jibna beida) or feta
Fresh bread rolls or crusty bread

steps.t: Tip the beans and their liquid into the saucepan and warm over medium-low heat for 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, until hot right through and very soft. Add a splash of water if they start to stick.

Mash the beans in the pan with the masher or the back of a wooden spoon to a coarse, creamy purée, leaving some beans whole. Sudanese ful is softer and looser than Egyptian, so add a little more hot water if needed until it slumps easily.
Stir in 2 tablespoons of the sesame oil, the cumin and the lime juice and season well with salt. Taste: the oil should give a gentle nutty flavour without overpowering the beans.
Spoon the ful into a wide bowl and drizzle with the remaining sesame oil. Pile the crumbled white cheese, tomato, onion, green chilli and rocket over the top in heaps rather than mixing them in.
Bring the bowl to the table with the bread. Sudanese families share ful from one dish, tearing off pieces of bread and using them to pinch up beans and toppings together.
For a fuller breakfast add sliced boiled eggs or a few ta'amiya (falafel), and serve sweet tea with milk on the side.

recipes.storage: The beans keep 3 days refrigerated without the toppings.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring, until steaming hot.
notes: Use light, untoasted sesame oil sold in Middle Eastern shops; dark toasted Asian sesame oil is far too strong here. Mild olive oil or a neutral oil also works.

recipes.name: Shiro wat (spiced chickpea flour stew)
recipes.description: The everyday stew of Ethiopia and Eritrea, and a fasting-day staple: shiro (spiced ground chickpea or pea flour) whisked into a base of slow-cooked red onion, garlic and berbere and simmered until thick, smooth and glossy.

ingredients.name: Oil (or niter kibbeh on non-fasting days)
Shiro powder (spiced chickpea or field pea flour), or chickpea flour
Salt
ingredients.prep: if your shiro powder is unsalted

steps.t: Put the chopped onions in the dry saucepan over medium heat, without any oil, and cook for 6–8 minutes, stirring often, until they soften, shrink and smell sweet; add a tablespoon of water if they start to catch. Dry-cooking onions this way is the base of most Ethiopian stews and gives a rich, smooth sauce.

Add the oil, garlic and ginger and cook for 2 minutes, then add the tomato and berbere and stir for 2–3 minutes more, until the tomato has melted into a deep red paste and the spices smell toasty. Keep the heat moderate so the berbere doesn't scorch.
Pour in about 600 ml of the hot water and bring to a simmer. Add the shiro powder a spoonful at a time, whisking constantly so that no lumps form, until it is all incorporated and the stew is smooth.

Turn the heat down to low and simmer for 10–12 minutes, stirring often with the wooden spoon and reaching right into the edges of the pan, as shiro catches easily. It will sputter, so partly cover the pan. Add the remaining water a little at a time if it gets thicker than a loose porridge.

The shiro is ready when it is glossy, thick enough to coat the spoon and no longer tastes floury, and a little oil has risen to the surface. Taste and add salt if needed, then lay the slit chillies on top and cook for 1 minute more.

Serve hot in a shallow bowl or ladled into the centre of a piece of injera, with gomen, salad or other wats around it. In Eritrea it is often served still bubbling in a small clay pot called a shiro tavita.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring well, until steaming hot.
notes: Ready-made shiro powder is sold in Ethiopian and Eritrean shops and already contains spices and salt; with plain chickpea flour, add 1 teaspoon each of extra berbere and garlic powder and ½ teaspoon of ground ginger.

recipes.name: Gomen (Ethiopian braised collard greens)
recipes.description: Collard greens slowly braised with onion, garlic, ginger and green chilli until silky and tender. A mild, fresh counterpoint to spicy wats on a platter of injera, and a staple of fasting days.
equipment: Large lidded pan or wide pot

ingredients.name: Oil (or niter kibbeh on non-fasting days)

steps.t: Wash the collards well in several changes of water. Strip the leaves from the tough central stems, stack and roll them up, and slice very finely, then chop across. Finely chopped greens cook evenly and turn silky.
Heat the oil in the pan over medium heat and cook the onion for 5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but not browned. Add the garlic and ginger and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the greens a few handfuls at a time, stirring each batch until it wilts before adding the next. Sprinkle with the salt and pour in the water.

Cover and cook over medium-low heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the greens are completely tender and dark green and most of the liquid has evaporated. Add another splash of water if the pan dries out before they are soft.
Stir in the chilli strips and the cardamom, if using, and cook uncovered for 2 minutes more. Taste for salt and serve warm or at room temperature with injera and wats.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: For gomen besiga, a festive version, brown 300 g of diced beef in the oil before adding the onion and simmer it until tender before the greens go in.

recipes.name: Siga tibs (Ethiopian sautéed beef with rosemary and chilli)
recipes.description: Cubes of beef seared fast and hot with red onion, rosemary, green chilli and spiced butter until browned outside and juicy inside. Ethiopia's favourite celebration and restaurant dish, ready in minutes.
equipment: Large heavy frying pan or cast-iron skillet

ingredients.name: Beef sirloin or rump
ingredients.prep: cut into 2 cm cubes, patted dry

ingredients.name: Niter kibbeh (Ethiopian spiced butter) or ghee

steps.t: Pat the beef cubes very dry with kitchen paper and season with the pepper; leave the salt until later so the meat browns instead of releasing its juices. Have all the vegetables cut and ready by the stove.

Heat the empty pan over high heat for 2 minutes until very hot, then add the oil and half the beef in a single layer. Sear without moving for 1½ minutes, then toss and cook for 1–2 minutes more until browned on several sides but still pink in the middle. Tip onto a plate and repeat with the remaining beef.

Lower the heat to medium-high and add the niter kibbeh, onion wedges, garlic and rosemary to the pan. Stir-fry for 3 minutes until the onion softens at the edges and the butter smells of herbs and spice.

Return the beef and its juices to the pan with the chilli strips, tomato, berbere and salt. Toss over high heat for 2–3 minutes until everything is glossy and sizzling, the tomato just softened, and the beef is cooked to your liking; Ethiopians traditionally like tibs a little pink in the centre.
Taste for salt and spice. Pick out the rosemary stalks if you like, but keep the leaves.
Serve straight away, ideally in a hot clay dish or skillet to keep it sizzling, with injera or bread, and a small dish of awaze (berbere paste) or mitmita for dipping.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat briefly in a hot pan until steaming; long reheating toughens the beef.

recipes.name: Injera (teff sourdough flatbread)
recipes.description: The spongy, slightly sour flatbread that is plate, spoon and bread at an Ethiopian or Eritrean meal. A simple batter of teff flour and water is fermented for two to three days, then cooked on one side only until covered in tiny holes.
equipment: Large non-stick frying pan with a lid (30 cm), or an electric mitad

ingredients.name: Dried yeast
ingredients.prep: only if you have no starter (ersho)

steps.t: Day 1: in the bowl, whisk the teff flour with the 750 ml of lukewarm water (and the pinch of yeast, or 3 tablespoons of liquid from a previous batch) until completely smooth. Cover loosely with a cloth and leave at warm room temperature, ideally 22–26 °C.

Leave the batter to ferment for 2–3 days without stirring. It is ready when a layer of yellowish liquid has formed on top, the batter below is full of bubbles and it smells pleasantly sour, like yoghurt. Carefully pour off and discard most of the liquid on top.

Stir in the salt and enough of the remaining water to make a thin batter, about the consistency of single cream or crêpe batter. Cover and leave for 30–60 minutes, until small bubbles appear on the surface again.

Heat the non-stick pan over medium heat until a drop of water dances on the surface; don't oil it. Pour about 125 ml of batter in a spiral, starting at the edge and working into the centre, then tilt the pan quickly to fill any gaps. The injera should be about 3 mm thick.

Cook for about 30 seconds until holes appear all over the surface, then cover with the lid and cook for 1½–2 minutes more. It is done when the surface is dry and set, the edges lift away from the pan and the underside is pale and smooth, not browned. Never flip injera.

Slide the injera onto a clean tea towel to cool, holey side up, and repeat with the remaining batter, wiping the pan with a dry cloth between injera. Don't stack them until completely cool, or they stick together.
Serve at room temperature: line a large tray with one or two injera, spoon wats and vegetables on top, and roll up the rest to tear and use for scooping.

recipes.storage: Wrap cooled injera in a cloth inside a plastic bag; keeps 2 days at room temperature, 5 days refrigerated, or 2 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: Serve at room temperature; warm refrigerated injera briefly in a covered pan or the microwave.
notes: Keep 3 tablespoons of the fermented batter in a jar in the fridge as ersho (starter) for the next batch; it shortens fermentation to about 1–2 days.
Many cooks outside Ethiopia mix teff with some barley, wheat or self-raising flour for a softer, quicker injera; 100% teff is traditional and gluten-free.

recipes.name: Sega wat (Ethiopian beef stew with berbere)
recipes.description: Also called key wat: beef simmered slowly in a deep red sauce of dry-cooked onions, niter kibbeh and plenty of berbere until tender and rich. A centrepiece of Ethiopian Sunday and holiday meals with injera.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Red onions
ingredients.prep: very finely chopped (a food processor helps)

ingredients.name: Niter kibbeh (Ethiopian spiced butter) or ghee

steps.t: Put the onions in the dry pot over medium heat with no fat. Cook for 15–20 minutes, stirring often, until they have lost most of their moisture, shrunk to about a third and turned soft, jammy and lightly golden. If they start to stick, add a tablespoon of water; this slow dry-cooking is what makes the sauce thick and smooth without flour.

Add the niter kibbeh and stir until melted, then add the berbere and tomato paste. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until the mixture is a deep brick red and smells rich and toasty; lower the heat if it begins to darken too much.
Add the garlic and ginger and cook for 2 minutes more, adding a splash of water if the paste catches.
Add the beef and stir well to coat every cube. Cook for 5 minutes, turning, until the meat has lost its raw colour on the outside.

Pour in the hot water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook over low heat for 60–75 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes, until the beef is very tender and the sauce has thickened and darkened, with a sheen of red butter on top. Add a little more water if it gets too thick; the sauce should coat the meat generously.
Stir in the cardamom, pepper and salt and simmer for 5 minutes more. Taste and adjust: the wat should be deeply spiced, with a lingering heat.
Rest for 10 minutes off the heat, then serve on injera with gomen, shiro or a fresh salad, and a spoonful of ayib (fresh cheese) to cool the heat.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen; the flavour deepens overnight.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Zigni (Eritrean beef stew)
recipes.description: Eritrea's best-loved stew: beef braised with plenty of onion, fresh tomato and berbere in oil until the sauce is thick, dark red and fragrant. Served with injera or kitcha bread, often with a boiled egg on the side.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid

steps.t: Cook the chopped onions in the dry pot over medium heat for 12–15 minutes, stirring often, until soft, reduced and starting to turn golden. Add a spoonful of water if they catch.
Add the oil and the berbere and fry for 3–4 minutes, stirring constantly, until the oil turns deep red and the spice smells toasty. Add the garlic and ginger and stir for 1 minute.
Add the tomatoes and tomato paste and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring and scraping the bottom, until the tomatoes break down completely into a thick, glossy paste and the oil separates at the edges.
Add the beef and stir to coat. Cook for 5 minutes until the cubes are sealed on the outside, then pour in the hot water and bring to a simmer.

Cover and simmer gently for 60–70 minutes, stirring every 15 minutes, until the beef is tender enough to cut with a spoon and the sauce is thick and coats the meat. Add a splash of hot water if it reduces too much before the meat is ready.
Stir in the cardamom and salt, plus the tesmi if using, and simmer 5 minutes more. Taste for salt and heat.
Serve hot on injera or with kitcha flatbread or crusty bread, with halved boiled eggs and a fresh tomato salad alongside.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Kicha fit-fit (torn flatbread with spiced butter)
recipes.description: An Eritrean breakfast favourite: a thick, unleavened kicha flatbread cooked in a pan, torn into pieces and tossed in warm butter spiced with berbere, then served with cool yoghurt. Ethiopians make a near-identical dish called chechebsa.
equipment: Large non-stick frying pan with a lid (26–28 cm)

ingredients.name: Spiced butter (tesmi), niter kibbeh or ghee

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt in the bowl and add the water gradually, stirring, to make a thick, sticky batter-like dough that just holds its shape; it should be softer than bread dough. Beat it with a spoon for 1 minute until smooth.
Heat the frying pan over medium heat and lightly oil it. Spread the dough evenly into the pan with wet fingers or the back of a spoon, about 1.5 cm thick, right to the edges.

Cover and cook for 7–8 minutes, until the underside is golden and the top has set and looks dry. Flip the kicha with the help of a plate and cook the second side, uncovered, for 6–7 minutes more, until golden and cooked through; it should sound hollow when tapped.
Tip the kicha onto a board, let it cool for a minute, then tear it into rough 2–3 cm pieces with your fingers.

Wipe out the pan and melt the spiced butter over low heat. Stir in the berbere for 20 seconds until fragrant, then add the torn kicha and toss for 1–2 minutes until every piece is coated in red butter and warmed through.
Pile into a bowl and serve hot with the yoghurt alongside (and a drizzle of honey if you like), to scoop up with each piece. Strong spiced tea or coffee is the traditional partner.

recipes.storage: Best fresh; plain kicha keeps 1 day wrapped at room temperature.
recipes.reheating: Toss leftovers in a hot pan with a little extra butter until warm.

recipes.name: Beef suqaar (Somali spiced beef stir-fry)
recipes.description: Small cubes of beef sautéed quickly with onion, peppers, tomato and xawaash, the warm Somali spice blend of cumin, coriander, cardamom and cinnamon. Eaten with rice, pasta or canjeero at any meal of the day.

ingredients.name: Beef sirloin or tender stewing steak

steps.t: Mix the cumin, coriander, cardamom, cinnamon, pepper and turmeric in the small bowl; this is a simple xawaash. Pat the beef dry and toss it with half the spice mix.

Heat the oil in the pan over high heat until shimmering. Add the beef in a single layer and stir-fry for 4–5 minutes, until browned on the outside. Cook it in two batches if your pan is small so it sears rather than stews.
Add the onion and garlic and stir-fry for 3 minutes, until the onion softens and turns translucent at the edges.
Add the green pepper, carrot, chilli, the remaining spice mix and the salt. Stir-fry for 3–4 minutes until the vegetables are just tender but still bright.

Add the tomato and a splash of water, lower the heat to medium and cook for 2–3 minutes, stirring, until the tomato softens into a light sauce that coats the meat. Check a cube: it should be cooked through and tender, with no raw centre.
Stir in the coriander and serve hot with lime wedges, alongside plain or spiced rice, Somali-style spaghetti, or torn canjeero for breakfast.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat briefly in a hot pan until steaming throughout.
notes: Lamb, goat or diced chicken thigh are cooked the same way; cook chicken until no pink remains.

recipes.name: Bariis iskukaris (Somali spiced rice with lamb)
recipes.description: Somalia's celebratory rice: basmati cooked in the spiced broth of tender lamb with onion, tomato, cardamom, cinnamon and cumin, finished with raisins. Served with a banana on the side and green chilli sauce, the Somali way.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

steps.t: Put the lamb in the pot with the water, half the cumin and 1 teaspoon of the salt. Bring to the boil, skim off the grey foam, then cover and simmer for 45 minutes, until the meat is tender. Lift out the meat and measure the broth: you need 850 ml, so top up with water or boil to reduce.
Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear, then soak it in cold water for 30 minutes and drain; soaked basmati cooks evenly and the grains stay long and separate.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 10–12 minutes, stirring, until soft and deep golden. Add the garlic, all the remaining spices and the cooked lamb and fry for 3 minutes, until the meat is coated and lightly browned and the spices smell warm and sweet.

Stir in the tomato and tomato paste and cook for 3 minutes until jammy. Tip everything into the large pot with the 850 ml of hot broth and the remaining salt and bring to the boil. Taste the broth: it should be well seasoned, a little saltier than you want the rice.

Stir in the drained rice and raisins, bring back to a lively boil and cook uncovered for 3–4 minutes, until the liquid has dropped to the level of the rice and small craters appear on the surface. Cover tightly (lay a clean cloth or foil under the lid) and cook on the lowest heat for 18–20 minutes without lifting the lid.
Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Remove the cinnamon stick, then fluff the rice gently with a fork, lifting the meat to the top.
Pile onto a large platter and serve with lime wedges, a banana for each person to eat alongside, and a green chilli and coriander sauce (basbaas) or a simple salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Canjeero (Somali sourdough pancakes)
recipes.description: Thin, spongy fermented pancakes, called laxoox in the north, cooked on one side only so the top is full of tiny holes. Eaten every morning with ghee and sugar, or with suqaar or beans, and sweet spiced tea.

ingredients.name: Fine white corn flour or sorghum flour

steps.t: Whisk the flour, corn flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the bowl, then gradually whisk in the warm water to make a smooth, thin batter, a little thinner than pancake batter. Cover and leave in a warm place overnight, or for at least 4 hours, until doubled, bubbly and pleasantly sour-smelling.
Stir the batter well. It should pour like single cream; whisk in a few tablespoons of water if it has thickened.
Heat the frying pan over medium heat until a drop of water sizzles away. Don't oil it. Pour a small ladleful (about 80 ml) into the centre of the pan.

Immediately use the base of the ladle to spread the batter outwards in a continuous spiral from the centre to the edge, making a thin pancake about 20 cm across with faint circular ridges. Work fast before it sets.
Cook for 1½–2 minutes without turning, until the top is covered in small holes and looks completely dry, and the underside is pale golden. If the top stays wet, cover the pan for 30 seconds.
Slide it onto a plate and repeat, stacking the canjeero as you go. Serve warm, drizzled with ghee and sprinkled with sugar, or alongside suqaar, beans or liver, with spiced Somali tea.

recipes.storage: Keep cooled canjeero wrapped for 1 day, or freeze in a stack for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm briefly in a covered dry pan or the microwave.
notes: The batter keeps 2 days in the fridge and gets more sour each day, which many people prefer.

recipes.name: Sukuma wiki (Kenyan braised greens with tomato)
recipes.description: Kenya's everyday greens, whose name means 'stretch the week': finely sliced collards or kale cooked quickly with onion and tomato until just tender. Eaten almost daily alongside ugali.
equipment: Large frying pan or wide pot

ingredients.name: Collard greens (sukuma) or kale
ingredients.prep: stems removed, leaves very thinly sliced

steps.t: Wash the greens, strip out the tough stems, then stack the leaves, roll them tightly and slice into very thin ribbons, about 3 mm wide. Fine shredding is the key: it lets the greens cook in minutes and stay bright green.
Heat the oil in the pan over medium heat and fry the onion for 4–5 minutes, stirring, until soft and just turning golden. Add the garlic (and chilli, if using) and stir for 30 seconds.
Add the tomatoes and the salt and cook for 3–4 minutes, pressing them with the spoon, until they collapse into a soft sauce.

Add the shredded greens and toss them through the tomato. Cook uncovered over medium-high heat for 4–6 minutes, stirring often, until wilted and tender but still a vivid green with a slight bite; don't cover the pan, or they turn dull and soggy.
Taste for salt and serve hot with ugali, chapati or rice, alongside beans, stewed beef or nyama choma.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat briefly in a pan until steaming; long reheating dulls the greens.
notes: Some cooks add a crumbled stock cube or a pinch of Royco seasoning with the tomatoes; use a vegetable stock cube to keep the dish vegan.

recipes.name: Ugali (stiff maize porridge)
recipes.description: The staple of Kenya and Tanzania: white maize flour cooked in boiling water and stirred hard until it forms a firm, smooth dome. Pinched off by hand, rolled into a ball and used to scoop up greens, stews and fish.

ingredients.name: Fine white maize flour (unga wa ugali)

steps.t: Bring the water and salt to the boil in the saucepan over medium-high heat. Whisk in about a third of the maize flour in a steady stream and keep whisking for 1–2 minutes until it thickens into a smooth porridge with no lumps.

Switch to the wooden spoon. Add the remaining flour a handful at a time, stirring hard after each addition. As the mixture stiffens, press it against the side of the pan and fold it over on itself, turning the pan with your other hand; hold the pan with a cloth, as it gets heavy.

Keep pressing and folding over medium-low heat for 6–8 minutes, until the ugali is thick, smooth and firm, comes away cleanly from the sides of the pan and smells of toasted maize. Add a little more flour if it is still soft, or a splash of water if it is too stiff to turn.
Gather it into a ball in the pan, cover and leave over the lowest heat for 2–3 minutes so it steams through and a thin crust forms on the bottom.

Turn the ugali out onto a plate, shaping it into a dome with the wet spoon. Serve hot: pinch off a piece, roll it into a ball in your palm, press a dent in it with your thumb and use it to scoop up sukuma wiki, stew, fish or nyama choma.

recipes.storage: Wrap leftovers and refrigerate for up to 2 days; ugali firms as it cools.
recipes.reheating: Slice and fry leftovers in a little oil until crisp, or steam until hot.
notes: The amount of flour varies with the brand; stop adding when the ugali feels firm and pulls away from the pan.

recipes.name: Nyama choma with kachumbari (Kenyan grilled goat)
recipes.description: Kenya's social meal: goat ribs or leg seasoned simply with salt, garlic and lemon and grilled slowly over charcoal until crisp outside and tender within, then chopped small and served with fresh kachumbari salad and ugali.
equipment: Charcoal grill or barbecue (or oven and grill)

steps.t: Rub the goat all over with the lemon juice, garlic, ginger, oil, salt and pepper. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight, then take it out 30 minutes before grilling.

Light the charcoal and let it burn down until covered with grey ash and glowing, with a medium heat: you should be able to hold your hand above the grill for 4–5 seconds. Bank the coals to one side so you have a hotter and a cooler zone.

Grill the goat over the cooler side, turning every 8–10 minutes, for 45–60 minutes, until deeply browned and crisp on the outside and cooked through to the bone. Move pieces over the hotter coals for the last few minutes to char the edges. Kenyans like nyama choma well done but still juicy.

Meanwhile, make the kachumbari: soak the sliced onion in cold salted water for 10 minutes to soften its bite, then drain. Mix with the tomatoes, chilli, coriander, lime juice and salt just before serving so it stays crisp.
Rest the meat for 5 minutes, then chop it on the board with the cleaver into small bite-sized pieces, bone and all, the way it is served at a Kenyan grill.
Pile the meat on a board with a little dish of salt mixed with chilli for dipping. Serve with the kachumbari, ugali or roasted green bananas, and sukuma wiki.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot oven or under the grill until sizzling and steaming hot.
safety: Cook goat until well browned outside with no pink juices at the bone; slow-cooked goat is safe once tender and steaming hot throughout.
notes: Without a charcoal grill, roast the goat at 180 °C for 60–75 minutes, turning once, then finish under a hot grill for 5 minutes to crisp the outside.
Beef short ribs or lamb ribs are grilled the same way.

recipes.name: Kenyan beef pilau
recipes.description: The coastal Swahili rice dish cooked for weddings, Eid and every big gathering: rice simmered in beef broth with deeply browned onions and toasted pilau masala of cumin, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon, with tender beef and potatoes.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid
Mortar and pestle or spice grinder

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into large chunks

steps.t: Put the beef in the medium pot with half the garlic and ginger, 1 teaspoon of the salt and the water. Bring to the boil, skim off the grey foam, then cover and simmer for 60 minutes, until the beef is tender. Strain and keep the broth; you need 850 ml, so top up with water or boil to reduce.

While the beef simmers, toast the cumin, cardamom, cloves and peppercorns in a dry pan over medium heat for 1–2 minutes, until fragrant and a shade darker. Crush them coarsely in the mortar; this is your pilau masala. Keep the cinnamon stick whole.

Heat the oil in the large pot over medium heat and fry the onions for 12–15 minutes, stirring often, until a deep, even brown but not burnt. The dark onions give Kenyan pilau its characteristic brown colour and sweet, rich flavour, so don't rush them.

Add the crushed masala, cinnamon stick and the remaining garlic and ginger and stir for 1 minute until very fragrant. Add the drained beef and potatoes and stir for 3 minutes to coat them in the spiced onions.

Add the drained rice and stir gently for 2 minutes so every grain is coated in oil. Pour in the 850 ml of hot broth, add the stock cube and the remaining salt and bring to the boil. Taste the liquid: it should be well seasoned.

Boil uncovered for 3–4 minutes, until the liquid has sunk to the level of the rice and small holes appear on the surface. Cover tightly, lay a cloth or foil under the lid if it isn't snug, and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes without stirring or lifting the lid.

Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Fluff gently with a fork, folding the beef and potatoes through. Serve with kachumbari (tomato, onion and chilli salad) and a hot chilli sauce such as pilipili.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Shop-bought pilau masala works well: use 1½ tablespoons instead of the whole spices.

recipes.name: Mandazi (Swahili coconut and cardamom doughnuts)
recipes.description: Lightly sweet, cardamom-scented doughnuts from the Swahili coast, made with coconut milk and fried until puffed and golden. Eaten at breakfast or teatime with spiced chai across East Africa.

steps.t: Mix the flour, sugar, yeast, cardamom and salt in the bowl. Pour in the lukewarm coconut milk and mix with your hand, adding the warm water a little at a time, until a soft dough forms that is not sticky.

Knead on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic; it should spring back slowly when pressed. Return to the bowl, cover and leave somewhere warm for about 1 hour, until roughly doubled in size.

Knock back the dough and divide it into four pieces. Roll each into a circle about 1 cm thick and cut into 8 wedges, like a pizza, or into squares. Lay them on a floured tray, cover and rest for 15 minutes so they puff up slightly.
Heat the oil in the deep pan, no more than one-third full, to 170 °C, or until a scrap of dough rises to the surface within a few seconds and sizzles steadily.

Fry 5–6 mandazi at a time for 2–3 minutes, turning them as soon as they puff up and float, until they are evenly golden brown all over. They should balloon and sound hollow; if they brown before puffing, the oil is too hot.
Lift out with the slotted spoon onto kitchen paper and cool slightly. Serve warm or at room temperature with chai, or alongside beans in coconut sauce for a coastal breakfast.

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight container for 2 days, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 160 °C oven for 5 minutes.
notes: For quicker mandazi without rising, replace the yeast with 1 tablespoon of baking powder and fry after a 15-minute rest.

recipes.name: Mchuzi wa samaki (Zanzibar coconut fish curry)
recipes.description: A Swahili-coast fish curry from Zanzibar: firm fish marinated in lime, garlic and turmeric, lightly fried, then simmered in a tomato and coconut milk sauce with curry spices and a tang of tamarind.
equipment: Wide frying pan or shallow casserole with a lid

ingredients.name: Firm white fish steaks or fillets (kingfish, snapper or grouper)

steps.t: Pat the fish dry and lay it in the shallow dish. Rub with the lime juice, crushed garlic, turmeric, chilli powder and salt, and leave to marinate for 15–20 minutes while you prepare the sauce ingredients; any longer and the lime starts to 'cook' the fish.

Heat the oil in the wide pan over medium-high heat. Fry the fish for 1½–2 minutes per side, until lightly golden and firm on the outside but not cooked through. Lift onto a plate; it will finish cooking in the sauce.
Lower the heat to medium and add the onion to the same oil. Cook for 6 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden. Add the minced garlic, ginger and chilli and stir for 1 minute.

Stir in the curry powder, cumin and turmeric and fry for 30 seconds until fragrant, then add the tomatoes and salt. Cook for 6–8 minutes, mashing with the spoon, until the tomatoes break down into a thick paste.
Stir in the tamarind and the coconut milk and simmer gently for 5 minutes, until the sauce is creamy and slightly thickened. Keep the heat low once the coconut milk is in so it doesn't split.

Slide the fish into the sauce in a single layer and spoon the sauce over. Cover and simmer very gently for 5–6 minutes, until the fish is opaque all the way through and flakes easily; avoid stirring, which breaks it up.
Taste the sauce for salt and sourness, scatter with coriander and serve hot with coconut rice (wali wa nazi), plain rice or chapati.

recipes.storage: Best fresh; refrigerate leftovers for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently, covered, until steaming hot throughout; avoid boiling.

recipes.name: Maharage ya nazi (beans in coconut sauce)
recipes.description: Red kidney beans simmered in a lightly spiced tomato and coconut milk sauce, a comforting everyday dish of the Tanzanian and Kenyan coast. Served with rice, chapati or mandazi.

steps.t: Heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat. Fry the onion for 5–6 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden. Add the garlic, ginger and chilli and stir for 1 minute until fragrant.
Add the curry powder and turmeric and stir for 30 seconds, then add the tomatoes and salt. Cook for 4–5 minutes, pressing with the spoon, until the tomatoes have broken down into a thick sauce.
Add the drained beans and stir to coat them in the tomato base. Mash a few beans against the side of the pan; this helps thicken the sauce.

Pour in the coconut milk and water, bring just to a simmer and cook gently, partly covered, for 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is creamy and thick enough to coat the beans. Don't let it boil hard or the coconut milk may split.
Taste for salt and chilli, stir in the coriander and serve hot with rice, chapati or mandazi.
Like most bean dishes it tastes even better the next day; loosen it with a splash of water when reheating.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: With dried beans, soak 250 g overnight, boil hard for 10 minutes, then simmer for 1–1½ hours until tender before using.

recipes.name: Rolex (Ugandan chapati and omelette roll)
recipes.description: Kampala's famous street breakfast, its name a play on 'rolled eggs': a vegetable omelette with cabbage, tomato and onion cooked on a griddle, laid on a soft layered chapati and rolled up tight.
equipment: Large flat frying pan or griddle

steps.t: Make the chapati dough: mix the flour and salt, add 2 tablespoons of oil and rub it in, then add the warm water gradually and knead for 5–7 minutes until soft, smooth and elastic. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Divide the dough into four balls. Roll one out to a thin circle, brush with oil, roll it up like a rope and coil it into a snail; this layering makes the chapati soft and flaky. Repeat, rest 5 minutes, then roll each coil out to a 22 cm circle.

Heat the frying pan over medium heat. Cook each chapati for about 1 minute until bubbles appear, flip, brush with a little oil and cook 1 minute, then flip again and press with the spatula until it puffs and has golden spots on both sides. Stack under a cloth to keep soft.
Mix the cabbage, tomato, onion, green pepper and salt. For each rolex, beat 2 eggs in a cup with a quarter of the vegetables.

Heat ½ tablespoon of oil in the pan over medium heat, pour in the egg mixture and spread it into a circle about the size of the chapati. Cook for 1½–2 minutes until the underside is set and golden, then flip and cook for 1 minute until the eggs are cooked through and no liquid egg remains.

Lay a chapati on top of the omelette in the pan for 20 seconds to warm it and stick the two together, then turn out, omelette side up. Roll up tightly, wrap the bottom half in paper and serve hot, with chilli sauce if you like. Repeat with the rest.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot; chapatis keep 2 days wrapped, or freeze for 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm leftover rolex in a dry pan for 1–2 minutes per side.
notes: Ready-made chapatis or large flour tortillas make this a 15-minute breakfast.

recipes.name: Chicken luwombo (chicken steamed in banana leaves)
recipes.description: The festive dish of the Buganda kingdom: chicken, tomato, onion and spices wrapped in parcels of softened banana leaves and steamed for two hours until meltingly tender and infused with the leaves' gentle aroma.
equipment: Banana leaves (fresh or frozen), or baking paper and foil
Large pot with a steaming rack or upturned heatproof plate
Gas flame or hot dry pan for softening leaves

steps.t: Soften the banana leaves: pass each leaf slowly over a gas flame or press it onto a hot dry pan for a few seconds, until it turns bright, glossy and pliable. Cut into 8 squares of about 40 cm and wipe them clean. Softened leaves fold without splitting.

Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium heat and lightly brown the chicken pieces for 6–8 minutes, turning, then lift out. In the same pan cook the onions for 5 minutes until soft, then add the garlic, ginger, curry powder and pepper and stir for 1 minute. This browning is a modern shortcut for extra flavour; traditionally everything goes into the leaves raw.
In a bowl, mix the chicken, onion mixture, tomatoes, green pepper, salt and water.

Lay two leaf squares on top of each other at right angles. Spoon a quarter of the chicken and sauce into the centre, gather the corners up into a pouch, twist and tie tightly with string, leaving no gaps for the sauce to escape. Make four parcels.

Line the base of the large pot with banana leaf trimmings or a rack and pour in water to just below the rack. Stand the parcels on top, cover tightly and bring to the boil. Steam over medium-low heat for 1½–2 hours, checking every 30 minutes and topping up with boiling water so the pot never runs dry.
Open one parcel carefully to check: the chicken should be falling from the bone, reach 74 °C, and sit in a rich, fragrant sauce. Re-tie and steam longer if needed.
Serve each person a parcel to open at the table, scattered with coriander, with steamed matoke (mashed green bananas), rice or sweet potatoes.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat in the parcels by steaming for 20 minutes, until steaming hot throughout.
notes: Beef, smoked fish, mushrooms or groundnut sauce are also cooked as luwombo the same way.
Without banana leaves, wrap each portion in a double layer of baking paper and then foil; the taste is milder but the method is the same.

recipes.name: Binyebwa (Ugandan groundnut sauce)
recipes.description: Uganda's beloved g-nut sauce: finely ground roasted peanuts simmered slowly with water, onion and tomato until thick, creamy and nutty, with a sheen of peanut oil. Ladled over matoke, sweet potatoes or rice.

ingredients.name: Roasted peanuts, unsalted
ingredients.prep: ground to a fine powder (or groundnut paste)

steps.t: Grind the peanuts in short bursts in the grinder until they are a fine powder, stopping before they turn into butter. In the saucepan, whisk the peanut powder with about 200 ml of the cold water to a smooth, lump-free paste, then whisk in the rest of the water.
Add the onion, tomatoes and salt and bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring constantly, as ground peanuts settle and catch quickly on the bottom of the pan.

Turn the heat down to low and simmer gently, partly covered, for 30–35 minutes, stirring every few minutes. The sauce will thicken, turn a deeper colour and lose its raw peanut taste; it is ready when a thin layer of oil appears on the surface and it smells toasty and nutty. Ugandan cooks say g-nut sauce must 'ripen' this way and shouldn't be rushed.
If the sauce gets thicker than double cream, whisk in a little hot water. Stir in the curry powder, if using, taste for salt and simmer 2 minutes more.
Serve hot ladled over steamed matoke, boiled sweet potatoes, cassava or rice, alongside greens. It is also the base of groundnut luwombo and of g-nut sauce with smoked fish.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring constantly, until steaming hot.
notes: Contains peanuts.
Unsweetened smooth peanut butter (200 g) can replace the ground peanuts; whisk it with hot water instead of cold.

recipes.name: Egusi soup (melon seed and leafy green stew)
recipes.description: One of Nigeria's best-loved soups: ground melon seeds fried in palm oil until they form rich, nutty curds, then simmered with peppers, beef and stock and finished with leafy greens. Eaten with pounded yam, eba or fufu.

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.prep: half chopped, half roughly cut for blending

steps.t: Put the beef, sliced onion, stock cubes, salt and 500 ml of the water in the medium pot. Cover and cook over medium heat for 10 minutes so the meat releases its juices, then add the remaining water and simmer for 40–50 minutes, until tender. Keep the stock: you need about 750 ml.

Meanwhile, blend the bell peppers, scotch bonnets and the roughly cut half onion to a coarse purée with a splash of water. In a bowl, mix the ground egusi with about 100 ml of water to make a thick paste.
Heat the palm oil in the large pot over medium heat for 2 minutes, until hot and fluid but not smoking (don't let it bleach pale). Add the chopped onion and fry for 2 minutes until fragrant.

Drop the egusi paste into the oil in small spoonfuls and leave it undisturbed for 2–3 minutes so lumps form, then stir gently and fry for 8–10 minutes, turning, until the egusi has set into soft, golden curds and smells toasty and nutty. Scrape the bottom often, as it catches easily.

Add the pepper purée and fry for 5 minutes, stirring, until the raw pepper smell has gone. Pour in the meat stock and add the beef, bring to a simmer, cover and cook gently for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the soup is thick and red oil rises to the top. Add a little water if it gets too thick.
Stir in the chopped greens and cook for 3–5 minutes, just until wilted and still bright green. Taste and adjust the salt and heat.
Serve hot with pounded yam, eba (garri), fufu or plain rice. To eat it the traditional way, pinch off a piece of the swallow, make a dent with your thumb and scoop up the soup.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Many cooks add 2 tablespoons of ground crayfish with the pepper base and pieces of smoked fish or stockfish with the meat, which give a deeper, smoky flavour.
Bitterleaf (washed of its bitterness) can replace some of the greens, as in Igbo homes.

recipes.name: Efo riro (Yoruba spinach and pepper stew)
recipes.description: A rich Yoruba stew of leafy greens 'stirred' into a fried base of red peppers, scotch bonnet and palm oil with tender beef. Bold, savoury and spicy, served with pounded yam, eba or rice.

steps.t: Put the beef, sliced onion, stock cubes, salt and 300 ml of the water in the medium pot. Cover and steam over medium heat for 10 minutes, then add the rest of the water and simmer for 40–50 minutes until tender. Keep about 300 ml of the stock.

Blend the bell peppers, scotch bonnets and the roughly cut half onion to a coarse purée; efo riro is best with some texture. Tip it into a saucepan and boil uncovered over medium heat for 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until most of the water has cooked off and the purée is thick.

Blanch the spinach: pour a kettle of boiling water over it in the colander, or dip it in boiling water for 30 seconds, then rinse with cold water and squeeze out as much liquid as you can with your hands. Squeezing stops the stew from turning watery.

Heat the palm oil in the large pot over medium heat for 2 minutes until hot but not smoking. Add the chopped onion and fry for 3 minutes until soft, then add the reduced pepper purée and fry for 10–12 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens, smells sweet rather than raw, and the oil separates on top.

Add the cooked beef and about 200 ml of the stock and simmer for 5 minutes so the meat takes on the pepper flavour. Taste the base and adjust the salt; it should be well seasoned because the greens will dilute it.
