Add the squeezed spinach and stir it through the sauce until every leaf is coated. Cook uncovered for 3–5 minutes, until the spinach is hot but still green. Add a splash more stock if it looks dry.
Serve hot with pounded yam, eba, amala or white rice, or alongside boiled yam or fried plantain.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 2 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Traditional additions include iru (fermented locust beans), ground crayfish, smoked catfish or stockfish and shaki (tripe); add them with the beef for a deeper flavour.

recipes.name: Akara (black-eyed bean fritters)
recipes.description: Crisp, airy fritters of skinned black-eyed beans blended with onion and scotch bonnet and whipped until fluffy, then fried until golden. A classic Nigerian Saturday breakfast with pap (ogi) or soft bread; Ghanaians call them koose.

ingredients.name: Onion
ingredients.prep: half roughly cut, half finely chopped

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.prep: as little as possible, for blending

steps.t: Soak the beans in cold water for 20–30 minutes, then rub handfuls vigorously between your palms to loosen the skins. Pour off the floating skins with the water, refill and repeat 4–5 times until the beans are almost all white. Then soak for 2 hours more (or overnight) to soften.

Drain the skinned beans and blend them with the roughly cut onion, scotch bonnet and only enough water to keep the blades moving, to a thick, very smooth paste. A thick paste is essential: a runny batter spreads and soaks up oil.

Tip the paste into the bowl and whisk it hard with a wooden spoon or a hand mixer for 3–5 minutes, until it lightens in colour, increases in volume and looks fluffy. This beating traps the air that makes akara light. Stir in the chopped onion and the salt just before frying.
Heat the oil in the deep pan, no more than one-third full, to 175 °C, or until a drop of batter sizzles and rises at once.

Scoop up heaped tablespoons of batter and slide them gently into the oil, frying 6–8 at a time. Fry for 2 minutes, then turn and fry 2–3 minutes more, until deep golden brown, crisp outside and fluffy and cooked through inside. Lift onto kitchen paper and let the oil return to temperature between batches.
Serve hot with warm pap (ogi or akamu), custard or soft agege bread split and stuffed with akara, and a pinch of pepper.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; keep leftovers refrigerated for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven or air fryer for 5–6 minutes.
notes: Skinning by hand takes time but gives the lightest akara; skinned bean flour (sold for moin moin and akara) is a quick alternative: mix it with water to a thick paste and beat well.

recipes.name: Puff-puff (Nigerian fried dough balls)
recipes.description: Soft, pillowy, lightly sweet yeasted dough balls with a hint of nutmeg, fried until golden. The party snack of Nigeria and West Africa, eaten warm at celebrations, as street food and with evening tea.

steps.t: Whisk the flour, sugar, yeast, nutmeg and salt in the bowl. Pour in the warm water gradually, beating with a wooden spoon or your hand, until you have a smooth, thick, sticky batter that falls from the spoon in a heavy ribbon; it should be wetter than bread dough but far thicker than pancake batter.
Beat for another 2 minutes to develop the gluten, then cover the bowl with cling film and a cloth and leave in a warm place for 45–60 minutes, until doubled in size, bubbly and wobbly.
Heat the oil in the deep pan, no more than one-third full, to 170 °C, or until a small drop of batter sinks briefly, then rises and sizzles steadily.

Without knocking out all the air, scoop up some batter with a wet hand, squeeze it up through the circle made by your thumb and forefinger, and use your other hand or a wet spoon to drop golf-ball-sized pieces into the oil. Or drop it from two wet spoons. Fry 8–10 at a time without crowding.

Fry for 3–4 minutes, turning the balls with the slotted spoon so they colour evenly, until puffed and golden brown all over. Many turn themselves over as they cook. Break one open to check that the centre is cooked and fluffy, not doughy.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve warm, plain or dusted with icing sugar. They are best within a few hours of frying.

recipes.storage: Keep in a covered container for 1 day, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 160 °C oven for 5 minutes.
notes: Ghana's bofrot and Cameroon's beignets are close cousins.

recipes.name: Goat meat pepper soup
recipes.description: A light but fiery Nigerian broth of bone-in goat simmered with scotch bonnet, ginger and aromatic pepper-soup spices, finished with scent leaves. Loved on cold evenings, at gatherings and as a remedy for colds.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or spice grinder

ingredients.name: Calabash nutmeg (ehuru), toasted and ground, or nutmeg

steps.t: Wash the goat pieces well. Put them in the pot with the onion, garlic, ginger, stock cubes and salt, cover and cook over medium heat for 10–15 minutes without water, stirring once or twice, so the meat steams in its own juices and absorbs the seasoning.

Pour in the water, bring to the boil and skim off the grey foam that rises to the surface for a clear broth. Lower the heat, cover and simmer gently for 60–75 minutes, until the goat is tender and pulls easily from the bone; goat varies, so older meat may need longer.

Meanwhile, if your pepper-soup spices are whole, toast them in a dry pan for 1–2 minutes until fragrant and grind them finely. Toast the calabash nutmeg seeds, crack off the shells and grind them too.

Stir the pepper-soup spice, nutmeg and scotch bonnet into the pot and simmer for 10 minutes more, until the broth is aromatic and peppery. Taste and adjust: it should be hot, savoury and well salted, with plenty of broth.
Add the shredded scent leaves, simmer for 1 minute and turn off the heat.
Ladle the meat and broth into deep bowls. Serve hot on its own, or with boiled white yam, plantain or white rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
safety: Cook goat until well browned outside with no pink juices at the bone; slow-cooked goat is safe once tender and steaming hot throughout.
notes: Pepper soup spice mixes (with calabash nutmeg, alligator pepper, uda and uziza) are sold ready-made in African shops.
For catfish pepper soup, simmer the broth with the spices for 15 minutes, then poach thick catfish steaks in it for 8–10 minutes.

recipes.name: Ghanaian jollof rice with chicken
recipes.description: Ghana's take on jollof: fragrant jasmine or basmati rice steamed in a spiced tomato and pepper base made with the stock from ginger-and-garlic seasoned chicken. Served with the chicken, shito and salad.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

ingredients.name: Jasmine or basmati rice
ingredients.prep: washed until the water runs clear

steps.t: Season the chicken with the ginger, garlic, grated onion, thyme, curry powder and one stock cube. Put it in the medium pot, cover and steam over medium heat in its own juices for 10 minutes, then add the water and simmer for 15 minutes. Lift out the chicken and keep the stock; you need about 800 ml.
Pat the chicken dry and brown it: roast at 220 °C for 20–25 minutes or fry in a little hot oil, turning, until golden and cooked through to 74 °C. Set aside, covered.

Blend the canned tomatoes, bell pepper, scotch bonnet and the half onion until smooth. Heat the oil in the large pot over medium heat and fry the sliced onion for 4 minutes until soft. Add the tomato paste and fry for 4–5 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens to a deep brick red.

Pour in the blended mixture with the bay leaves, the second stock cube and the salt. Cook uncovered for 15 minutes, stirring often, until reduced by about a third, the raw pepper smell has gone and red oil rises to the surface.

Stir in the washed rice until every grain is coated, then pour in 700 ml of the chicken stock and bring to the boil. Taste the liquid: it should be well seasoned. Cover the pot with foil and the lid and cook on the lowest heat for 20 minutes without stirring.

Scatter the carrot and green beans over the rice, sprinkle with a few tablespoons of stock if the rice looks dry or is still firm, cover again and cook for 8–10 minutes more, until the rice is tender and separate. Turn off the heat and rest 5 minutes.
Remove the bay leaves, fluff the rice gently with a fork and serve with the chicken, shito (black pepper sauce), fried plantain and a fresh salad.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Ghanaian cooks use aromatic jasmine or basmati rather than the parboiled long-grain rice favoured in Nigeria, and season the base with more ginger and garlic.

recipes.name: Waakye (Ghanaian rice and beans)
recipes.description: A beloved Ghanaian breakfast and lunch from the north: rice and black-eyed beans cooked together with dried sorghum leaves that stain them a deep reddish brown. Served with a spicy tomato stew, shito, boiled eggs, gari and fried plantain.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a tight lid

ingredients.name: Dried black-eyed beans or red cowpeas
Bicarbonate of soda (or a handful of waakye leaves)
Long-grain rice
ingredients.prep: washed until the water runs clear

steps.t: Soak the beans overnight in plenty of cold water, then drain and rinse. If you have waakye leaves (dried sorghum leaf sheaths), rinse them well and tie them in a bundle.

Put the beans and the waakye leaves (or the bicarbonate of soda) in the pot with the water. Bring to the boil, then simmer, partly covered, for 40–50 minutes, until the beans are almost tender and the water has turned a deep wine-red. The colour is the mark of good waakye.
Check the liquid: it should cover the beans by about 3 cm. Add the washed rice and the salt, stir once and add hot water if needed so the liquid sits about 1.5 cm above the rice.

Bring back to the boil, then cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 20–25 minutes without stirring, until the rice has absorbed the liquid and is tender, and the beans are soft but still whole. If the rice is still firm, sprinkle over a little hot water, cover and give it 5 minutes more.
Turn off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Remove the leaves and fluff the rice and beans together gently with a fork; they should be a uniform reddish brown.
Serve the waakye on a plate (or on a leaf, the street-food way) with Ghanaian tomato stew, shito, halved boiled eggs, a sprinkle of gari, fried plantain, salad and, often, a little boiled spaghetti.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Waakye leaves are sold dried in African shops; bicarbonate of soda gives a similar colour and softens the beans but adds no flavour, so use only a little.

recipes.name: Red red (black-eyed bean stew with fried plantain)
recipes.description: Ghana's much-loved budget lunch, named for its colour: black-eyed beans in a red palm oil, tomato and chilli sauce, served with sweet fried ripe plantain and a sprinkle of gari.

ingredients.name: Very ripe plantains (yellow with black spots)

steps.t: Drain the soaked beans, put them in the pot with the water and bring to the boil. Simmer, partly covered, for 35–45 minutes, until completely tender and creamy inside but not falling apart. Drain, keeping about 200 ml of the cooking water.

Meanwhile, heat the palm oil in the frying pan over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until hot. Add the onions and fry for 6–8 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden. Add the garlic, ginger and scotch bonnet and stir for 1 minute.
Add the tomato paste and fry for 2 minutes until it darkens, then add the blended tomatoes and salt. Simmer for 10 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce is thick and the oil rises to the surface.

Tip in the beans with a splash of their cooking water and fold them gently through the sauce. Simmer for 5–8 minutes over low heat, stirring carefully, until the sauce coats the beans and some have softened into it. Mash a few with the spoon if you like a thicker stew. Taste for salt.

For the plantain, peel and cut into 1.5 cm diagonal slices. Heat the oil in a clean frying pan to about 1 cm deep over medium heat (about 170 °C). Fry the slices in batches for 2–3 minutes per side, until deep golden and caramelised at the edges. Drain on kitchen paper and sprinkle with a little salt.
Serve the beans in bowls with the fried plantain alongside and a sprinkle of gari on top for crunch.

recipes.storage: The bean stew keeps 3 days refrigerated; fry the plantain fresh.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: With canned black-eyed beans (2 × 400 g, drained), skip step 1 and the dish is ready in 30 minutes.
Many Ghanaians add a little smoked fish or ground dried shrimp to the sauce.

recipes.name: Kelewele (spiced fried plantain)
recipes.description: Accra's night-market favourite: cubes of ripe plantain tossed with fresh ginger, chilli, onion and warm spices, then fried until caramelised and crisp at the edges. Served hot with roasted peanuts.

ingredients.name: Ripe plantains (yellow with black spots)
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 2 cm cubes

steps.t: In the bowl, mix the ginger, grated onion, cayenne, cloves, nutmeg, salt and water into a loose paste. Add the plantain cubes and toss gently with your hands until every piece is coated. Leave for 10–15 minutes so the spices soak in.
Heat the oil in the frying pan or wok, about 4 cm deep, to 175 °C, or until a cube of plantain sizzles vigorously at once.

Fry the plantain in two or three batches for 4–5 minutes, turning occasionally, until deep golden brown and caramelised at the edges but still soft inside. Ripe plantain is full of sugar and darkens quickly, so lower the heat a little if it browns before it softens.
Lift out with the slotted spoon onto kitchen paper, let the oil come back to temperature and fry the next batch.
Serve hot in a paper cone or bowl with roasted peanuts on the side, as a snack or alongside red red, jollof or grilled fish.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot; it softens as it cools.
notes: Riper plantains give sweeter, softer kelewele; firm yellow ones hold their shape better.

recipes.name: Thiéboudienne (Senegalese fish and rice)
recipes.description: Senegal's national dish, born in Saint-Louis: fish steaks stuffed with a parsley, garlic and chilli paste, simmered in a tomato broth with cabbage, cassava, carrots and aubergine, then broken rice cooked in the rich broth until it forms a prized crust.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or small food processor
Large heavy pot (6 litres) with a lid

ingredients.name: Firm white fish steaks, bone-in (thiof, grouper or sea bream)
Cassava
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into large chunks

ingredients.name: Broken jasmine rice (riz brisé)
ingredients.prep: rinsed until the water runs clear

steps.t: Make the rof: pound or blend the parsley, garlic, spring onions, scotch bonnet, pepper and crumbled stock cube to a coarse green paste. Cut two deep slits in each side of every fish steak and push a little rof into each slit; keep the rest of the paste.

Heat the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat. Fry the fish steaks for 2–3 minutes per side until golden but not cooked through, then lift out. In the same oil, fry the onions for 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden.

Lower the heat, add the tomato paste and the remaining rof and fry for 8–10 minutes, stirring constantly and scraping the bottom, until the paste turns dark brick red and the oil separates. This long frying gives thiéboudienne its depth, so don't hurry it.

Pour in the hot water, add the second stock cube, the tamarind, the whole scotch bonnet and the salt and bring to the boil. Add the cassava, carrots and cabbage and simmer, partly covered, for 15 minutes.

Add the aubergine, pumpkin and okra and lay the fish on top. Simmer gently for 15–20 minutes more, until the fish is opaque and flakes at the bone and the vegetables are tender. Lift the fish and vegetables out as they are done into a dish, cover with a ladle of broth and keep warm. Remove the scotch bonnet.

Measure the broth: you need about 1 litre for the rice; set any extra aside as sauce. Bring the 1 litre back to the boil, stir in the rinsed rice and taste for salt. Cover tightly and cook over low heat for 25–30 minutes, stirring once after 15 minutes, until the rice is tender and has absorbed the broth.
Turn the heat up to medium for the last 3–5 minutes without stirring so a golden, crisp layer forms on the bottom of the pot. This crust, the xooñ, is the cook's treat and is served separately.
Spread the rice on the platter, arrange the vegetables and fish on top and spoon over some of the reserved broth. Serve with lime wedges and the crisp xooñ, eaten communally from the platter.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Traditional cooks add a piece of guedj (fermented dried fish) and yeet (fermented sea snail) with the tomato paste for a pungent, savoury depth; they are sold in West African shops.
For thiébou yapp, make the same dish with lamb or beef instead of fish.

recipes.name: Poulet yassa (chicken with lemon and caramelised onions)
recipes.description: A Casamance classic loved across Senegal: chicken marinated in lemon, mustard, garlic and chilli, grilled until charred, then simmered in a tangy sauce of slowly softened onions. Served with plain white rice.
equipment: Large heavy pot or deep frying pan

ingredients.name: Chicken legs and thighs, bone-in, skinned

steps.t: In the bowl, mix the sliced onions, lemon juice, mustard, garlic, scotch bonnet, pepper, stock cube, salt and 1 tablespoon of the oil. Add the chicken, rubbing the marinade into the meat. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight, turning once.

Lift the chicken out of the marinade, scraping the onions back into the bowl; keep the onions and all the liquid. Grill the chicken over hot coals, on a hot griddle pan or under a hot oven grill for 6–8 minutes per side, until well browned and charred in spots; it doesn't need to be cooked through yet.

Meanwhile, drain the onions, keeping the marinade liquid. Heat the remaining oil in the large pot over medium heat and add the onions. Cook for 20–25 minutes, stirring often, until very soft, sweet and golden; they should melt down rather than fry crisp, so lower the heat if they colour too fast.
Pour the reserved marinade liquid and the water over the onions, add the bay leaves and bring to a simmer. Taste: the sauce should be sharp with lemon and mustard and well salted.

Nestle the grilled chicken into the onions, cover and simmer gently for 20–25 minutes, turning once, until the chicken is tender, reaches 74 °C at the bone and the sauce has thickened. Add the olives for the last 5 minutes, if using.
Remove the bay leaves and serve hot, spooning plenty of onions and sauce over the chicken, with a mound of plain white rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Discard any marinade that isn't boiled in the sauce: it has been in contact with raw chicken.
Fish yassa is made the same way with whole grilled fish or thick fish steaks; simmer them for only 8–10 minutes.

recipes.name: Mafé (Senegalese peanut stew with beef)
recipes.description: West Africa's great peanut stew as cooked in Senegal and Mali: beef simmered in a tomato and peanut butter sauce with carrots, sweet potato and cabbage until rich and velvety. Served over white rice.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Beef chuck or stewing beef (or lamb shoulder)
Sweet potato or cassava
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into large chunks

steps.t: Heat the oil in the pot over medium-high heat. Brown the beef in two batches for 4–5 minutes per batch, turning, until well coloured on several sides, then lift out. Browning in batches keeps the pan hot so the meat sears instead of boiling.

Lower the heat to medium, add the onions and cook for 6–8 minutes until soft and golden, scraping up the browned bits. Add the garlic and tomato paste and fry for 3 minutes, stirring, until the paste darkens.

Return the beef to the pot. In a bowl, whisk the peanut butter with about 400 ml of the hot water until smooth, then stir it into the pot with the remaining water, the stock cube, whole scotch bonnet, bay leaf and salt.
Bring to a gentle simmer, partly cover and cook over low heat for 45 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes and scraping the bottom, as peanut sauces catch easily.

Add the carrots and sweet potato, tucking them under the sauce, and simmer for 15 minutes. Add the cabbage wedges and simmer for 10–15 minutes more, until the beef is very tender, the vegetables are soft and the sauce is thick, with a layer of reddish oil on top. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.
Remove the scotch bonnet (burst it into the sauce first if you want more heat) and the bay leaf, and taste for salt. Serve hot over white rice, with the vegetables arranged on top.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring, until steaming hot.
notes: Contains peanuts.

recipes.name: Bissap (hibiscus and mint iced drink)
recipes.description: Senegal's ruby-red national drink: dried hibiscus flowers steeped with fresh mint, sweetened and chilled. Tart, floral and refreshing, sold in plastic bags on Dakar streets and served at every celebration.

steps.t: Rinse the dried hibiscus flowers in a sieve under cold water to remove any dust. Bring the water to the boil in the large saucepan.

Add the hibiscus and mint to the boiling water, then take the pan off the heat. Cover and leave to steep for 10–15 minutes, until the liquid is a deep, dark crimson. Longer steeping makes it more tart and slightly bitter.
Strain through the fine sieve into the jug, pressing gently on the flowers to extract the liquid, then discard the flowers and mint.

Stir in the sugar while the liquid is still warm until completely dissolved, then add the vanilla or orange-blossom water, if using. Taste: bissap should be sweet-tart and intensely flavoured, as it will be served over ice.
Cool, then chill in the fridge for at least 2 hours. Serve very cold, over ice, garnished with a mint sprig.

recipes.storage: Keeps 5 days in a covered jug in the fridge; shake before serving.
notes: Dried hibiscus is sold as bissap, flor de jamaica or sorrel in African, Latin American and Caribbean shops.

recipes.name: Thiakry (millet couscous with sweet yoghurt)
recipes.description: A cool, creamy Senegalese dessert: fine millet couscous steamed until fluffy, then folded into sweetened yoghurt and cream with vanilla, nutmeg and raisins. Served chilled for celebrations and Tabaski.
equipment: Steamer or couscoussier (or a fine sieve over a pot)

steps.t: Spread the millet couscous in a wide bowl and sprinkle with about 100 ml of the water, rubbing it between your fingers to moisten every grain evenly and break up any clumps.

Bring water to the boil in the base of the steamer. Line the steamer basket with a damp cloth if its holes are large, add the millet loosely and steam, uncovered, for 10 minutes from the moment steam rises through the grains.

Tip the millet back into the bowl, sprinkle with the remaining water and the butter and rub again to separate the grains. Steam for 8–10 minutes more, until tender and fluffy with no hard centre. Spread out and leave to cool completely.
In the large bowl, whisk the yoghurt, crème fraîche, sugar, condensed milk, vanilla and nutmeg until smooth and the sugar has dissolved.

Fold the cooled millet and the raisins into the yoghurt mixture. Taste and add a little more sugar if you like. The thiakry should be thick and spoonable; loosen with a little milk if it is too stiff.
Cover and chill for at least 1 hour so the millet softens and absorbs the cream. Serve cold in small bowls or glasses, with an extra grating of nutmeg on top.

recipes.storage: @chilled
notes: Instant millet couscous only needs moistening with boiling water, covering for 5 minutes and fluffing with a fork.

recipes.name: Attiéké with poisson braisé (cassava couscous with grilled fish)
recipes.description: The everyday feast of Abidjan's maquis: whole fish marinated in garlic, ginger, onion and chilli and grilled until charred, served with attiéké (tangy fermented cassava couscous), fresh tomato-onion salad and a hot pepper sauce.
equipment: Charcoal grill, griddle pan or oven grill

ingredients.name: Whole tilapia or sea bream (2 fish), scaled and gutted
Attiéké (fermented cassava couscous), fresh or frozen
Scotch bonnet peppers
ingredients.prep: very finely chopped, for the pepper sauce

steps.t: Blend or pound the half onion, garlic, ginger, parsley, deseeded scotch bonnet, stock cube, lemon juice, 2 tablespoons of the oil and the salt to a paste. Cut 3 deep diagonal slashes on each side of the fish and rub the paste all over and into the cuts and cavity. Marinate in the fridge for 30 minutes to 2 hours.
Heat the grill to medium-hot (or the oven grill to high with a rack 10 cm below). Brush the grill bars or a foil-lined tray with the remaining oil so the skin doesn't stick.

Grill the fish for 8–12 minutes per side, depending on thickness, until the skin is blistered and charred in places and the flesh at the thickest part near the bone is opaque and flakes easily, or reads 63 °C. Turn only once, carefully, with a wide spatula.

Meanwhile, make the salad by mixing the tomatoes, sliced onion and cucumber with the lime juice, a pinch of salt and the tablespoon of oil. For the pepper sauce, mix the chopped scotch bonnets with a spoonful of the salad juices and a pinch of salt.

Warm the attiéké: steam it for 5–8 minutes until hot and fluffy, or put it in a covered bowl with a tablespoon of water and microwave for 3–4 minutes, stirring halfway. Fluff with a fork and season lightly with salt.

Serve each person a mound of attiéké with half a fish (or a whole small one), the tomato and onion salad on top or alongside, and the pepper sauce to add at the table. Eat with your fingers, maquis-style.

recipes.storage: Best eaten fresh; refrigerate leftover fish and attiéké separately for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the fish in a hot oven until steaming hot; steam the attiéké.
notes: Attiéké is sold fresh, frozen or dried in African shops. Dried attiéké should be rehydrated with an equal volume of water before steaming.
Mackerel and other oily fish are also popular for poisson braisé.

recipes.name: Kedjenou (Ivorian slow-cooked chicken in a sealed pot)
recipes.description: A Baoulé classic: chicken and vegetables cooked in their own juices with no added water in a tightly sealed pot, traditionally a clay canari, shaken rather than stirred. Tender, concentrated and gently spicy.
equipment: Heavy casserole with a very tight lid (or a canari)
Foil or a flour-and-water paste to seal the lid

ingredients.name: Scotch bonnet or bird's eye chillies

steps.t: Put the chicken, onions, tomatoes, aubergine, green pepper, garlic, ginger, chillies, thyme, bay leaves, stock cube and salt into the casserole and mix well with your hands so the seasoning coats every piece. Kedjenou needs no water and traditionally no oil: everything cooks in the juices of the chicken and vegetables.
Cover with a sheet of foil and press the lid down hard on top, or seal the lid with a rope of flour-and-water paste, so that no steam can escape. A tight seal is the whole secret of the dish.
Set the pot over medium heat until you hear it begin to sizzle and bubble inside, about 8–10 minutes, then lower the heat to low.

Cook for 50–60 minutes without opening the lid. Every 10 minutes, hold the lid down firmly with a cloth and shake the pot vigorously from side to side for a few seconds, so the contents turn over and don't stick. If you smell any scorching, lower the heat.

After about an hour, open the pot carefully, away from your face. The chicken should be very tender and reach 74 °C at the bone, and sit in a thick, concentrated sauce made from the vegetables. If it is too thin, simmer uncovered for 5 minutes.
Remove the bay leaves, taste for salt and serve hot with attiéké, white rice or foutou (pounded plantain).

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Guinea fowl, the original meat for kedjenou in Baoulé villages, is cooked the same way and takes about 20 minutes longer.

recipes.name: Ndolé (bitterleaf, peanut and prawn stew)
recipes.description: Cameroon's national dish from the Douala coast: washed bitterleaf greens simmered in a creamy sauce of boiled ground peanuts with beef and prawns, then crowned with fried onions and prawns. Served with plantain, miondo or rice.

steps.t: Simmer the beef with the sliced half onion, crushed garlic, stock cubes, salt and water, covered, for 50–60 minutes until tender. Keep the beef in its stock.

Meanwhile, put the peanuts in a saucepan, cover with water and boil for 20 minutes until softened. Drain, then blend with the chopped onion, garlic, ginger, scotch bonnet and about 300 ml of fresh water to a smooth, pourable cream.

If using bitterleaf, wash it repeatedly: squeeze handfuls under running water, then boil for 10 minutes, drain and squeeze again, until only a pleasant bitterness remains. Chop kale finely and blanch it with the spinach for 1 minute; squeeze dry.

Pour the peanut cream into the large pot with the beef and about 400 ml of its stock. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium-low heat and cook for 20 minutes, stirring often and scraping the bottom, as it sticks easily, until it thickens, turns from white to light beige and tastes cooked, not raw.
Stir in the squeezed greens and simmer for 10 minutes more, stirring, until the sauce is thick and creamy and clings to the leaves. Add a splash of stock if it gets too thick and taste for salt.
In the frying pan, heat the oil over medium-high heat and fry the thinly sliced onion for 5–6 minutes until golden. Add the prawns and fry for 2–3 minutes, until pink and opaque all the way through.
Pour half the hot oil, onions and prawns into the ndolé and stir through. Spoon the rest on top to serve, with boiled or fried ripe plantain, miondo or bobolo (cassava sticks) or white rice.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 2 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently with a splash of water, stirring, until steaming hot.
notes: Contains peanuts.
Pre-washed frozen or dried ndolé is sold in African shops; spinach and kale give a milder but very good version.
Smoked fish or ground dried crayfish are often added with the peanut cream.

recipes.name: Poulet moambé (Congolese chicken in palm sauce)
recipes.description: Congo's national dish: chicken browned and simmered in a rich, orange-red sauce of palm fruit with onion, garlic, tomato and chilli, enriched with a little peanut butter as many Kinshasa cooks do. Served with rice, fufu (luku) or saka-saka.
equipment: Large heavy pot or casserole with a lid

steps.t: Season the chicken with the salt and pepper. Heat the palm oil in the pot over medium-high heat until hot and fluid. Brown the chicken in batches for 5–6 minutes per batch, turning, until golden on all sides, then lift out.

Lower the heat to medium, add the onions to the red oil and cook for 6–8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute, then add the tomatoes and tomato paste and cook for 5 minutes, pressing with the spoon, until they collapse into a thick sauce.
Whisk the peanut butter with about 200 ml of the hot water until smooth, then stir it into the pot with the remaining water and the stock cube.

Return the chicken and its juices to the pot, add the whole chilli and bring to a gentle simmer. Cover and cook over low heat for 30–35 minutes, turning the chicken and stirring the bottom every 10 minutes, until the chicken is tender and reaches 74 °C at the bone.

Uncover and simmer for 5–10 minutes more, until the sauce is thick, glossy and coats the chicken, with a layer of orange oil on top. Stir in the spinach for the last 2 minutes, if using. Taste for salt and remove the chilli.
Serve hot with white rice, fufu (luku) or chikwangue (cassava bread), and saka-saka (cassava leaves) or other greens on the side.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Contains peanuts.
For the traditional palm-nut version, replace the palm oil and peanut butter with 400 g of canned palm-nut cream (sauce graine / noix de palme) and simmer 10 minutes longer.

recipes.name: Bobotie (Cape Malay spiced mince bake)
recipes.description: South Africa's beloved Cape Malay bake: minced beef gently curried with onion, turmeric and dried fruit, softened with milk-soaked bread, then topped with a savoury egg custard and bay leaves and baked until golden. Served with yellow rice.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Tear the bread into a bowl, pour over half of the 250 ml of milk and leave to soak while you cook the mince.

Heat the butter and oil in the frying pan over medium heat and cook the onions for 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden. Add the garlic, curry powder and turmeric and stir for 1 minute until fragrant; the spices should smell warm, not scorched.
Add the mince and cook over medium-high heat for 6–8 minutes, breaking it up with a wooden spoon, until it has lost its pink colour and any liquid has evaporated.

Squeeze the soaked bread lightly and mash it into the mince with the rest of its milk, the apricots, raisins, brown sugar, vinegar, salt and pepper. Simmer for 3 minutes, then taste: bobotie should be gently spiced and balanced between sweet and sour. Adjust with sugar, vinegar or salt.

Spread the mince in the baking dish and press it down evenly with the back of a spoon. Whisk the eggs with the remaining milk (the other half of the 250 ml plus the 150 ml) and a pinch of salt and pour it gently over the meat. Roll the bay leaves slightly and stand them in the custard, and scatter with almonds if using.
Bake for 30–35 minutes, until the custard is set, puffed and golden brown on top and a knife pushed into the centre comes out without liquid egg. The filling should be piping hot.
Rest for 5 minutes, then cut into squares and serve with yellow rice (rice cooked with turmeric, cinnamon and raisins), fruit chutney and a sliced tomato and onion sambal.

recipes.storage: Keeps 3 days refrigerated or 2 months frozen.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Many Cape cooks stir 2 tablespoons of apricot jam or fruit chutney into the mince instead of the dried apricots and sugar.

recipes.name: Bunny chow (Durban lamb curry in a bread loaf)
recipes.description: Durban's famous street meal: a fiery Durban-Indian lamb and potato curry ladled into a hollowed-out quarter loaf of white bread, with the scooped-out bread on top for dipping. Eaten with the hands, with grated carrot salad.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Durban masala (hot red curry powder)
ingredients.prep: or less for a milder curry

ingredients.name: Potatoes
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into 4 cm chunks

steps.t: Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat. Add the cinnamon, cardamom, star anise and fennel seeds and fry for 30–60 seconds until they sizzle and smell fragrant, then add the curry leaves, standing back as they spit. Blooming whole spices in oil this way carries their flavour through the whole curry.

Add the onions and cook for 8–10 minutes, stirring, until soft and golden. Stir in the garlic and ginger for 1 minute, then add the Durban masala, garam masala and turmeric with a splash of water and fry for 1 minute, stirring, so the spices cook without burning.

Add the lamb and stir to coat. Cook for 8–10 minutes over medium-high heat, turning, until the meat is sealed and the masala clings to it. Add the tomatoes and salt and cook for 5 minutes until they break down and the oil starts to separate.

Pour in the hot water, bring to a simmer, cover and cook gently for 40 minutes. Add the potatoes and simmer, covered, for 20–25 minutes more, until the lamb is tender and the potatoes are soft and starting to thicken the gravy. The curry should be thick and saucy, not watery; simmer uncovered for a few minutes if needed.
Meanwhile, make the carrot sambal by mixing the grated carrot with the green chilli, vinegar and a pinch of salt and sugar.

Cut the loaf into quarters across. With a small knife and your fingers, hollow out each quarter, leaving walls about 1.5 cm thick and keeping the scooped-out bread (the 'virgin') in one piece if you can.

Stir the coriander into the curry, remove the cinnamon and star anise, and ladle the curry and potatoes into the bread, letting the gravy soak into the walls. Top each with its virgin and serve at once with the carrot sambal. Eat with your hands, tearing the bread from the top down.

recipes.storage: Keep the curry refrigerated for up to 3 days or freeze for 3 months; fill the bread only when serving.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Durban masala is a hot, deep red curry powder sold in South African shops; a mix of 4 teaspoons Kashmiri chilli powder and 2 teaspoons of medium curry powder is a good substitute.
Bean (sugar bean) and chicken bunnies are also classics.

recipes.name: Chakalaka (spicy vegetable and bean relish)
recipes.description: A spicy township relish born in Johannesburg: onion, peppers, carrot, tomato and baked beans cooked with curry powder and chilli. Served hot or cold with pap, bread and anything from the braai.
equipment: Large frying pan or wide pot

steps.t: Heat the oil in the pan over medium heat. Fry the onion for 5 minutes until soft and translucent, then add the garlic, ginger and chillies and stir for 1 minute.
Add the curry powder and paprika and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant, adding a splash of water if they start to catch.
Add the peppers and grated carrots and cook for 5–6 minutes, stirring, until they begin to soften but still have some crunch.
Stir in the tomatoes, salt and sugar and simmer for 8–10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce has thickened and the vegetables are tender.
Add the baked beans with their sauce and heat through gently for 3–4 minutes. Taste and adjust with salt or more chilli; chakalaka should be tangy and hot.
Serve warm or at room temperature with pap, bread or rice, and with braaied meat, boerewors or grilled fish.

recipes.storage: Keeps 4 days refrigerated; it is often made a day ahead and served cold.
notes: Some cooks add diced cabbage, cauliflower or a little grated ginger and lemon juice; a can of chickpeas or butter beans can replace the baked beans.

recipes.name: Stywe pap (South African stiff maize porridge)
recipes.description: The everyday staple across South Africa: white maize meal steamed and stirred into a firm porridge that holds its shape. Served with chakalaka, tomato and onion gravy, stews and meat from the braai.

steps.t: Bring the water and salt to a rolling boil in the saucepan. Pour the maize meal into the centre all at once so it forms a mound; don't stir yet.
Cover, reduce the heat to low and leave for 5 minutes, so the meal steams and the water bubbles up around the mound.

Uncover and stir vigorously with the fork or wooden spoon, breaking up all the lumps and pressing them against the side of the pan, until the pap is evenly mixed and fairly stiff. If it is too dry to stir, add a few tablespoons of boiling water.

Cover again and cook over the lowest heat for 15–20 minutes, stirring well every 5 minutes, until the pap is firm, smooth and no longer tastes raw or gritty. Long, slow steaming is what distinguishes good pap.
Stir in the butter, if using. For krummelpap (crumbly pap), use only 500 ml of water and stir with a fork rather than a spoon, so it stays in dry, fluffy crumbs.
Shape the stiff pap with a wet spoon into balls or a mound and serve hot with chakalaka, a tomato and onion relish, stew or braai meat.

recipes.storage: Keeps 2 days refrigerated.
recipes.reheating: Steam leftovers until hot, or slice and fry in a little oil.

recipes.name: Malva pudding (South African apricot sponge with cream sauce)
recipes.description: A soft, caramelised sponge flavoured with apricot jam, baked until golden and then soaked with a hot butter, cream and sugar sauce until it is sticky and moist. South Africa's favourite Sunday pudding, served warm with custard.

steps.t: Heat the oven to 180 °C and butter the ovenproof dish.
Whisk the eggs and sugar with the electric whisk for 4–5 minutes until thick, pale and fluffy and the whisk leaves a trail when lifted. Beat in the apricot jam.

Mix the melted butter, vinegar and milk in a jug. Sift the flour, bicarbonate of soda and salt together. Fold the flour and the milk mixture alternately into the egg mixture in three additions, mixing gently until just smooth; the batter will be quite runny.

Pour into the buttered dish and bake for 35–40 minutes, until well risen, deep golden brown on top and a skewer pushed into the centre comes out clean. The top should be quite dark and caramelised; that is how it should be.

While the pudding bakes, put the cream, butter, sugar and hot water in the saucepan and heat gently, stirring, until the butter has melted and the sugar has dissolved. Stir in the vanilla and keep warm; don't let it boil.

As soon as the pudding comes out of the oven, prick it all over with a skewer or fork and slowly pour the hot sauce over the top, letting it soak in before adding more. It will look like too much sauce, but the sponge absorbs it all in about 10 minutes.
Serve warm with hot custard, cream or vanilla ice cream.

recipes.storage: @chilled
recipes.reheating: Warm portions in the microwave or a low oven until heated through.

recipes.name: Melktert (South African milk tart)
recipes.description: A cherished Afrikaner and Cape Malay tart: a crisp, sweet shortcrust filled with a light, wobbly custard of milk, cinnamon and vanilla, finished with a generous dusting of cinnamon. Served at room temperature or chilled with tea.
equipment: Tart tin or pie dish, 23 cm
Baking beans or rice and baking paper

ingredients.name: Ground cinnamon
ingredients.prep: mixed with 1 tsp sugar, to dust

steps.t: Make the pastry: mix the flour, baking powder and salt, then rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar, add the beaten egg and bring it together into a soft dough without kneading. Wrap and chill for 20 minutes.

Heat the oven to 190 °C. Roll the pastry out on a floured surface to about 4 mm thick and line the tin, pressing it into the edges and trimming the top. Prick the base with a fork, line with baking paper and fill with baking beans or rice.

Bake for 15 minutes, then remove the paper and beans and bake for 8–10 minutes more, until the pastry is golden and crisp all over. Blind-baking keeps the base from going soggy under the custard. Let it cool while you make the filling.

Heat the milk with the cinnamon stick and butter in the saucepan over medium heat until steaming and just coming to the boil, 6–8 minutes. Meanwhile, whisk the sugar, flour, cornflour and eggs in a bowl to a smooth paste.

Remove the cinnamon stick. Pour about a third of the hot milk into the egg mixture while whisking constantly; this is called tempering and stops the eggs from scrambling. Pour it all back into the pan with the rest of the milk.

Cook over medium-low heat, whisking constantly and reaching into the corners of the pan, for 5–7 minutes, until the custard thickens, starts to bubble gently and no longer tastes floury; it should be thick enough to coat the whisk heavily. Stir in the vanilla.

Pour the hot custard into the pastry case and smooth the top. Dust generously with the cinnamon sugar while it is still warm, then cool to room temperature and chill for at least 2 hours until set. Cut into slices with a hot knife and serve cool or at room temperature.

recipes.storage: @chilled
notes: For a quick crustless version, pour the custard into a dish lined with Marie biscuits instead of pastry.
